Mahomes bounced back to a top-two fantasy finish last season, but the rebound was driven almost entirely by a spike in rushing rather than his passing, which has quietly declined for years. Even with a Week 1 return expected, that matters because a torn ACL and LCL makes it unlikely he runs as much this season, removing the exact thing that fueled his 2025 value. Add in an aging Travis Kelce, a possible Rashee Rice suspension and a down year from Xavier Worthy, and there's real risk, though the return of coordinator Eric Bieniemy from Mahomes’ peak years offers upside. He's worth drafting in single-quarterback leagues but should be paired with a second option to stream by matchup.

At his best, Mahomes is the league's best quarterback. He averaged 26.1 fantasy points per game in 2018 despite only 272 rushing yards and two rushing touchdowns. He finished first again in 2022 and was a clear-cut fantasy starter in every year between. He fell outside the top 10 fantasy quarterbacks in 2023 and 2024 before jumping back to a tie for second last season.

Part of that decline came with a drop in passing grade. He posted three seasons at 89.0 or better in his first five years as a starter, then slid steadily to 70.7 last season. His average target depth fell from 9.5 at his peak to 6.8 and 6.9 in 2023 and 2024. It climbed back to 8.3 last season, which helped his yards per attempt and yards per game, but also brought more negatively graded and less accurate throws.

The big reason for his fantasy bounce-back was his rushing. He ran once more per game than the previous season, averaged 1.3 more yards per carry and scored three more touchdowns. That added 2.5 fantasy points per game, while his passing rose by just 0.3.

Mahomes then suffered a torn ACL and LCL. Signs point to him playing in Week 1, but he is unlikely to keep running as much as he did last season because of the injury. There are also question marks around his receivers, as Travis Kelce is another year older, Rashee Rice could face a suspension at some point, and Xavier Worthy had a down year.

The good news is that Eric Bieniemy is back as offensive coordinator. He held the role from 2018 to 2022, when Mahomes was at his fantasy best. If Kansas City returns to the offense that made him a fantasy star and MVP, that could lift his production despite the concerns.

In single-quarterback leagues, Mahomes should be drafted alongside another option, so whoever has the best matchup that week can slot into your lineup.

Stafford is coming off an MVP season and the fourth-most fantasy points per game, but his production leaned heavily on a career-best touchdown rate and career-low interception rate that are strong regression candidates. Stafford was the league's MVP last season. He led the league in passing yards per game at 276.9, only slightly above his career average. His 7.9 yards per attempt tied for the third-best mark of his career. What really set him apart statistically was his touchdowns and interceptions. He threw a touchdown on 7.7% of his passes, a career high, and an interception on just 1.3%, a career low outside of his 2010 season, when he played only three games.

All of that added up to the fourth-most fantasy points per game at 21.1, but significant regression is fair to expect. If his touchdown rate falls back to his 2023 rate, his best season from 2022 to 2024, he would have averaged 4.3 fewer fantasy points per game, which would have put him at QB18. He coincidentally finished as QB18 that season.

Stafford's age, 38, is also a concern. His play clearly didn't regress last season, but at some point a decline is inevitable. There is also a chance Los Angeles is simply too good this season. The Rams led the league in points scored but ranked only 10th in points allowed. They added Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson to the defense, and there are at least rumors that Aaron Donald could join them. If that defense improves as expected, the Rams won't need to throw as much and will spend the fourth quarter running the ball with backups.

Stafford might only belong in fantasy starting lineups in weeks the game projects to be close, which means he shouldn't be drafted as a starter in single-quarterback leagues. He is also a notable case of a quarterback ranked much lower in dynasty than in redraft, given his age.

Monangai was a seventh-round pick by the Bears in 2025. Typically, not much is expected from seventh-round running backs, but Monangai quickly overtook Roschon Johnson and Travis Homer to become the second running back on the Bears’ depth chart. Chicago eased him into action in September, but after the Week 5 bye, he consistently played at least 20 offensive snaps and ran at least five times each week.

Monangai received double-digit carries in seven games, including every game from Weeks 11 to 15. Like several backup running backs, his attempts partially depended on game script. He averaged 11.5 carries per game in victories and 7.0 in losses.

Chicago didn't make any notable acquisitions to the running back room, so we will likely have another season with Monangai sharing time with D'Andre Swift. Swift graded notably better as a runner, receiver and pass-blocker last season, so it wouldn't be shocking to see a similar split this season.

Monangai averaged 10.4 PPR points per game from Week 6 until the end of the season, ranking 30th-best among running backs. Ideally, he improves as a player, but that could be offset by the loss of Drew Dalman at center and more carries going to wide receivers.

Monangai's value in fantasy drafts will vary widely by league type. Several running backs ranked near him are very high-risk, high-reward given the uncertainty around their roles. Monangai is relatively safe in his role and doesn't carry as much risk, but he also doesn't have as much upside.

If only 20 to 24 running backs are starting in a fantasy league in any given week, Monangai won't have much value, because he won't typically be worth a starting spot unless Swift suffers an injury. It would generally be better to select a running back who has better odds of finishing as a top-20 back.

If 28 to 36 running backs are starting in a given league, he has much more value, because he would be a weekly starter in that league.

Sutton has been Denver's top receiver and a touchdown machine under Sean Payton, tallying the sixth-most receiving scores in the league over the past three seasons. The question is a crowded room: The Broncos traded for Jaylen Waddle and still have three young receivers they've invested in, and Payton has a long history of rotating the position. At 31 with a strong grade chasm behind Waddle and a rookie in Pat Bryant capable of pushing him at X, Sutton's volume could erode, and Denver may move on after the season. He remains a touchdown-dependent flex option, with his outlook tied largely to how the rotation shakes out.

Sutton has spent most of the past seven seasons as the top receiver in the Broncos' offense. He missed nearly all of 2020 with an injury, and in 2022, Jerry Jeudy ended up with more yards. But that role did not lead to much fantasy success until Sean Payton took over as head coach and turned Sutton into a touchdown machine. Sutton’s 25 receiving touchdowns over the past three seasons rank sixth among all wide receivers, and he has finished 26th and 21st in fantasy points per game the past two years.

Denver has spent several high draft picks on young receivers recently, taking Marvin Mims Jr. in 2023, Troy Franklin in 2024 and Pat Bryant in 2025, and none has cut into Sutton's playing time so far. The Broncos didn't draft a receiver this year, but they traded their first-round pick for Jaylen Waddle. Waddle owns a 90.0 PFF receiving grade over the past three seasons, 12th among all wide receivers, while Sutton's 80.7 ranks 32nd.

At 6-foot-3 and 216 pounds, Sutton has fit nicely as an X receiver throughout his career, while Waddle is more of a Z and slot. The two could coexist fine on their own, but the complication is that Denver still has the three young receivers it believes in, and Payton has a long history of rotating his receivers.

Franklin and Mims will likely rotate in the slot and take a few snaps from Waddle at Z. Bryant began his career as Sutton's backup at X, playing there throughout the preseason, and only saw more time once he moved to Z. It is entirely possible Bryant shifts back to X and cuts further into Sutton's snaps.

Sutton signed an extension a year ago but will turn 31 early in the season, and the Broncos could move on from him after the year if Bryant plays well enough. To find out whether Bryant is ready, they have to give him the reps.

The one reason Sutton remains a flex option is his scoring history, and even then, he projects as a frustrating, touchdown-dependent play. Normally, a starting receiver doesn't gain much when a backup goes down. But in Denver, an injury to any of the depth receivers could lift the playing time and target share of everyone else.

He was acquired in part because of the Travis Hunter injury but ended up taking over as the Z receiver.

From Weeks 12 to 18, Meyers led Jacksonville's receivers in routes and receptions, but Parker Washington filled Hunter's slot role and paced the group in receiving yards. Meyers ranked 24th in fantasy points per game over that stretch, while Washington was 11th.

The best case is that Meyers stays the Z receiver in both two- and three-receiver sets with a normal starter's workload. An offseason to learn the offense and build chemistry with Trevor Lawrence should sharpen his efficiency, putting a top-20 fantasy season within reach.

Washington has emerged as the team's best receiver, and if he and Hunter are on the field together, that could push Meyers off it. Goff has been remarkably durable and productive in raw passing terms, leading all quarterbacks in passing yards over the last four years. Still, his complete lack of rushing production has kept him outside the fantasy QB1 range in most of those seasons despite strong weapons and an excellent supporting cast. Without rushing upside, even a big statistical season likely caps Goff in the same range as Tom Brady‘s heavy-volume 2021, which only produced a QB3 finish. Goff is best treated as a streaming option rather than a draft-and-hold starter, valuable to pair with another quarterback and deploy on the best matchups each week.

Goff has spent the last five seasons as the Lions' starting quarterback and hasn't missed a game in the last four seasons. He's finished the last four seasons in the QB6-QB10 range in total points, but has finished outside the top 12 quarterbacks in fantasy points per game in three of those four seasons.

His 85.0 passing grade over the last four seasons is 10th-best among quarterbacks. His passing production has been elevated by his coaching staff, skill players and offensive line. Goff has thrown for 18,205 yards over the last four years, the best mark among quarterbacks by over 1,000 yards. He's accomplished this despite Patrick Mahomes and Justin Herbert having more dropbacks.

Goff was one of three quarterbacks last season with over 4,000 passing yards but fewer than 100 rushing. Most of Goff's official rushing attempts were either kneel downs or fumbles. His only designed runs for positive gains were three sneaks, and he scrambled five times. The lack of rushing production puts a major damper on his high-end fantasy value. The last quarterback to average over 22 fantasy points per game with fewer than 200 rushing yards was Tom Brady in 2021, and he posted the third-most passing attempts in a season in NFL history to reach enough fantasy volume. Brady only finished at QB3 that season.

Quarterbacks like Matthew Stafford, Goff and Sam Darnold, who have great receivers in high-scoring offenses, aren't being drafted as starters in single-quarterback leagues, because it's more likely their passing volume decreases than increases, and there isn't much reason to expect notable increases in rushing production. Quarterbacks with more rushing upside are generally favored in other high-scoring offenses. However, Goff is one of several quarterbacks who are great to pick up late, pair with another solid fantasy option, and start whichever quarterback has the best matchup that week.

Goedert has been a reliable fantasy tight end for years, finishing top 12 in points or points per game every season since his second, mostly on volume that gave him a high floor and low ceiling. His 2025 campaign was the worst of his career by most measures, with career lows in PFF receiving grade (69.7), yards per game (39.4), yards per reception, yards after catch and big-play rate. Goedert stayed fantasy-relevant only because of a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns, but that total rests on extreme outliers: Eight came inside the 6-yard line (tied for the most by a tight end in 20 years) and five arrived via shovel passes and wide screens (more than double any tight end over that span), which makes heavy regression likely. With the Eagles drafting Eli Stowers to cut into his snaps and Sean Mannion taking over as offensive coordinator, Goedert will need both a bounce-back in quality of play and continued scheme help to avoid sliding into bye-week fill-in territory.

Goedert has a long history of reliability in fantasy football. He finished as TE10 in his second NFL season and has concluded top 12 in either fantasy points or fantasy points per game in every subsequent season.

For most of his career, he accomplished this through volume, giving him a high floor and low ceiling. From 2019 to 2024, Goedert posted the sixth-most receiving yards among tight ends but only the 12th-most touchdowns. He also posted the seventh-best PFF receiving grade by a tight end during this span at 87.8.

Goedert was 30 years old during the 2025 season, and by several measures, it was the worst of his career. His 69.7 receiving grade was a career low, and his 39.4 receiving yards per game was the worst mark since his rookie season. His 9.8 yards per reception and 4.1 yards after the catch per reception were career lows, as was his 0% contested catch rate.

Most notably, Goedert stopped making as many big plays. He earned a +1 grade or better on at least 1.5% of his routes in each of his first four career seasons. That rate fell to the 1.1-1.3% range from 2022 to 2024, and to 0.5% last season.

He was able to counteract this from a fantasy perspective with a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns, more than doubling his previous high of five. Eight of those scores came when the Eagles were within 6 yards of scoring, tied for the most by a tight end in a season over the last 20 years. Jimmy Graham matched that mark in 2017. No tight end has finished a season with seven such touchdowns, and only six have reached six.

Moreover, five of Goedert's touchdowns came on shovel passes and wide screens, and no other tight end in the last 20 years has more than two touchdowns from that combination of routes in a season. All of this makes it highly likely that Goedert's touchdown total regresses. The Eagles drafted Eli Stowers in the second round to be their tight end of the future. While it's unlikely Stowers overtakes Goedert in 2026, he could cut into Goedert's playing time more than recent Eagles backups have.

To remain a weekly fantasy starter, Goedert will need to bounce back in his quality of play and have his new offensive coordinator, Sean Mannion, scheme up touchdowns the way Kevin Patullo did. Some combination of continued regression with age, a decrease in snaps in favor of Stowers and a return to his usual touchdown totals would be enough to make Goedert only a bye-week fill-in.

Okonkwo has averaged 1.46 yards per route run over the last four years, which is tied for 10th-best among tight ends with at least 1,000 routes. Where he's really stood out is his play after the catch. His 5.8 yards after the catch per catch are tied for third-best among tight ends, behind George Kittle and Jonnu Smith.

While he's been good enough on a per-route basis to be a high-end TE2, Okonkwo hasn't run enough routes, and he hasn't scored enough touchdowns. He's finished at TE21 each of the last three seasons. While Okonkwo sports the 19th-most routes for a tight end over the last four years, he’s run the 40th-most routes within the 5-yard line, and he’s garnered only two targets in those situations.

He replaces Zach Ertz, who ended last season on injured reserve, while John Bates will be the primary blocking tight end, and Ben Sinnott is expected to take more of an H-back role. Ertz was TE7 as recently as 2024 in Washington's offense.

Expectations for Okonkwo will be higher than they were for Ertz at ages 34 and 35. Given the uncertainty at wide receiver outside of McLaurin, Okonkwo is the favorite to finish second on the team in targets. This gives him a solid floor, making him a low-end TE2.

His ability to turn into a TE1 will largely depend on the quality of the Commanders' offense in general. It's unlikely Okonkwo becomes a frequent target near the goal line, given his lighter size for a tight end, but a few more touchdowns than usual are a possibility.

Okonkwo is one of the ideal targets at tight end for someone who wants to focus entirely on running backs and wide receivers earlier in the draft and punt on the position.

Tuten is the likeliest to lead the group in fantasy points given his dual-threat role, but Rodriguez's efficiency and bigger frame could earn him goal-line work in a potentially high-scoring offense. He fell to fourth on the depth chart in 2024 behind Robinson, Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols, leaving him without a role for most of the season. His carry total dropped to 35, but he stayed effective, averaging 4.9 yards per attempt.

He again looked like the odd man out in 2025 after Jacory Croskey-Merritt was drafted in the seventh round. But Robinson was traded, Ekeler was hurt early in the season and Croskey-Merritt's efficiency declined, opening the door for Rodriguez to take over the starting job in Week 10. He missed two games late in the year with an injury but had double-digit carries in each of his final five.

Rodriguez has averaged 3.6 yards after contact per carry over the past three years, second-best among running backs with at least 150 carries. His 28.3% first-down rate also ranks second, and his 0.25 avoided tackles per attempt are tied for fifth. He has earned a +1.0 rushing grade or better on 6.6% of his carries, the third-highest rate behind Raheem Mostert and Jahmyr Gibbs. His rushing efficiency suggests he could be an excellent fantasy back with more volume, but the Commanders never used him as a receiver, as he caught just six passes in 35 career games.

Rodriguez signed with the Jaguars in free agency, reuniting with his former college coach, Liam Coen. He will compete for playing time with Bhayshul Tuten and LeQuint Allen. Tuten has the best chance to lead the team in fantasy points as the one back most likely to see significant volume as both a rusher and a receiver, but Rodriguez has been the more efficient runner. He is also notably bigger than Tuten and Allen, which could earn him goal-line carries in what may be a high-scoring offense.

There is a chance Tuten leads the Jaguars' backfield in fantasy points, and also a chance the offense plays well enough to support two fantasy-relevant backs. That makes Rodriguez an intriguing late-round option.

Mitchell flashed elite potential as a rookie with the Ravens, averaging 8.4 yards per carry over a six-week stretch before an ACL injury derailed his development. He arrives in Los Angeles with the highest PFF grade of the Chargers' three-back room over the past three seasons despite his down 2024 campaign. The key factor is his fit with new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who brought Mitchell to Los Angeles himself, while Hampton and Vidal are holdovers. Mitchell shares the same rare size-speed profile as McDaniel's previous featured back De'Von Achane, with both sitting at 5-foot-8 or shorter and 200 pounds or lighter while posting sub-4.40 40-yard dash times. If McDaniel ultimately prefers Mitchell over his other options, the upside is top-10 at the position.

Mitchell entered the league as an undrafted rookie with the Baltimore Ravens in 2023 and received his first carry in Week 9 of his rookie year. Over the following six weeks, he recorded 47 carries for 396 yards and two touchdowns, averaging 8.4 yards per carry and at least 6.0 in five of those six games. A significant ACL injury late in 2023 sidelined him for much of 2024 and clearly affected his play upon his return. By 2025, he had settled in as Derrick Henry‘s primary early-down backup, averaging 5.8 yards per carry on a limited 4.5-carry per-game workload.

Mitchell signed with the Los Angeles Chargers this offseason, joining a backfield that also includes 2025 first-round pick Omarion Hampton and Kimani Vidal, who played well in Hampton‘s absence last season. Despite his down 2024 campaign, Mitchell earned the highest PFF grade of the trio over the past three seasons, including the top receiving grade.

He is also the running back most closely tied to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel's preferred archetype. McDaniel brought Mitchell to Los Angeles himself, while Hampton and Vidal are holdovers. More importantly, Mitchell most closely resembles McDaniel's previous featured back, De'Von Achane. Achane, Mitchell, and Jaleel McLaughlin are the only running backs 5-foot-8 or shorter and 200 pounds or lighter to log at least 300 snaps over the past three seasons. That group joins Isiah Pacheco, Ty Chandler, Latavius Murray, and former McDaniel back Raheem Mostert as the only backs to run both a sub-4.40 40-yard dash and a sub-1.50 10-yard split at the combine while recording at least 300 snaps in a season.

Given those similarities to Achane, there is a real chance McDaniel ultimately prefers Mitchell over his other options. If Mitchell approaches Achane's level of production, he offers top-10 upside at the position.

Shaheed has built a career as an explosive, boom-or-bust deep threat, with big plays and touchdowns offset by frequent quiet games, and a meniscus tear ended his 2024 early. A 2025 trade sent him to Seattle to reunite with coordinator Klint Kubiak, though his role and average depth of target dipped there. The Seahawks changed coordinators again but signed him long-term, and there is real buzz he could leap Cooper Kupp to become the clear second option behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba. He is a high-upside late-round pick, with the bonus that his fantasy outlook should clarify within the first month or two.

Shaheed went from undrafted rookie to All-Pro returner in his second season. His offensive playing time grew as his rookie year progressed, including three late games with 75 or more receiving yards. He played more than 50% of snaps and became more of a deep threat in his second season, with six games over 60 yards, five of which included a touchdown, and nine games of 36 yards or fewer, with nothing in between.

In 2024, Shaheed leaned even further into the deep-threat role, with an 18.8 average depth of target and a 39% deep-target rate. He made eight explosive plays over six games, gaining 73 or more yards in four of them and 11 or fewer in two others, before a meniscus tear ended his season early.

Shaheed was off to a much more consistent start in 2025, with four or more receptions in each of his first nine games. He was in the final year of his contract, and the Saints did not plan to re-sign him long-term, so they traded him to the Seattle Seahawks. Seattle had lost its third receiver, Tory Horton, for the season, and Seahawks offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak had been Shaheed's coordinator in 2024.

His playing time was inconsistent in Seattle. He had two games over 60 receiving yards and ran the ball more than he caught it during the playoffs. His average depth of target fell to 11.5, down from his previous stint in Kubiak's offense.

Seattle changed offensive coordinators again but still signed Shaheed to a long-term contract. There is significant speculation that he is in line for a larger role this season, presumably passing Cooper Kupp on the depth chart to become the second option in the passing game behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Shaheed is a fine, high-upside late-round option. Unlike most younger late-round targets, we should have a good read on whether he will pay off in fantasy after the first month or two of the season.

Strange took over as Jacksonville's starter after outplaying Evan Engram. Rookie second-round pick Nate Boerkircher was added mainly to handle blocking and free up Strange as a receiver, and the latter held up as a starter last season even with most of a talented receiver room healthy. His ceiling is capped by that receiver depth, so a top-five finish is unlikely. But his ADP is that of a mid-range backup, making Strange a strong value with borderline-starter potential given his talent and quarterback.

Strange was a second-round pick in 2023. He served as a rotational backup as a rookie but experienced a four-game stretch as a starter early in the season and another four-contest run late with Evan Engram injured. He averaged 8.3 PPR points per game across that span, which included three games with at least 60 yards, two with a touchdown and three with minimal production. He graded just as well as Engram, so Jacksonville let Engram leave in free agency and made Strange the full-time starter.

Last season, Strange averaged 9.3 fantasy points per game over the first four weeks, putting him at TE14, before a quad strain early in Week 5 led to a six-game absence. He returned immediately with a five-reception, 93-yard game. He also scored three touchdowns and averaged 11.1 PPR points per game over that seven-game stretch, 12th among tight ends.

The Jaguars spent a second-round pick on Nate Boerkircher, which could mean a slight dip in snaps, but the plan is for Boerkircher to do the dirty work as a blocker and free up Strange as a receiver.

Jacksonville has plenty of talent at receiver in Parker Washington, Brian Thomas Jr., Jakobi Meyers and Travis Hunter. But three of those four were healthy at the end of last season, and Strange still played well enough to be a fantasy starter down the stretch.

Strange is unlikely to become a top-five fantasy tight end given the Jaguars' receiver talent, but his ADP is that of a mid-range backup. He has the talent and quarterback to finish more like a borderline starter.

With Walker gone, Charbonnet’s competition is now Jadarian Price, George Holani and Emanuel Wilson. Charbonnet’s upside is an early return to full form and a bigger role, but the likelier outcome is diminished effectiveness for much of the year and a role similar to last season's.

Charbonnet spent the first three seasons of his career as the Seahawks' receiving back, playing roughly 50% of snaps in each. He started six games in 2024 with Kenneth Walker III injured and was excellent for fantasy, running 14 or more times in five of them while averaging a touchdown and over three receptions per game.

In 2025, Charbonnet was consistently the goal-line back, leading to 12 rushing touchdowns. Seattle's commitment to the run would usually be enough to produce a top-10 fantasy back, but the team split the work enough between Walker and Charbonnet that it was hard to trust either. Both averaged 11.3 PPR points per game, tied for 28th among running backs.

Charbonnet tore his ACL in the divisional round of the playoffs, which makes it very likely he misses the start of the season. He did some work off to the side during OTAs, putting him ahead of schedule, though being ready to play does not guarantee he will be as effective as he was before the injury.

Once he's back, he will no longer have Walker to compete with. Instead, first-round rookie Jadarian Price, backup George Holani and free-agent addition Emanuel Wilson are competing for the playing time.

The ideal case for Charbonnet is that he returns early in the season, plays at his pre-injury level, and sees a larger role than he did alongside Walker. The more likely scenario is that he isn't as effective for much of the season and his role looks similar to last year's.

Henry was a boom-or-bust tight end for most of his Patriots tenure. The concerns for 2026 are his age, now 31, and added target competition from A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. A season-ending injury to blocking tight end Julian Hill also leaves the room thin enough that New England could add another body. Henry profiles as a low-upside backup, best as a fill-in if a starter gets hurt or a riskier early pick busts.

Henry has spent the past five years as the Patriots' lead tight end after five seasons with the Los Angeles Chargers. Through his first three years with New England, he mixed a few high-ceiling games with several in which his role in the offense was minimal.

He had three games with 75 or more yards in his first season, and 42 or fewer in the other 14. In his second, he had two games with 60 or more yards and a touchdown but was held under 22 yards in over half his games. 2023 was a similar mix, three games with 50 or more yards and a touchdown, but under 30 in half of them.

Once Drake Maye became the quarterback, Henry grew more reliable, trading some of his low-end games for a new ceiling. In both 2024 and 2025, he had two games with seven or more receptions for 90 or more yards. He had reached 90 yards just three times in his first eight seasons.

He finished 16th in fantasy points per game in 2024 and 13th in 2025. The concerns are that he is 31 and could begin to decline, and that the Patriots added A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs, which could cut into his target rate. They also swapped blocking tight ends, losing Austin Hooper and adding Julian Hill, but Hill then suffered a season-ending injury, so it would not be surprising if New England adds another tight end at some point.

Henry is a low-upside backup option, a fine fill-in if a starter gets hurt or if a riskier tight end drafted earlier doesn't pan out.

Tracy has started 23 of a possible 34 games over the last two seasons for New York, which is impressive for a former fifth-round pick. He posted four weeks as a top-10 fantasy running back during his rookie season and added two weeks as a top-five back over the last month of last season.

Tracy had lost his starting job last season to Cam Skattebo before Skattebo's season-ending injury. Skattebo is expected to be ready for Week 1 and is the likely starter for New York this season. The Giants have a new coaching staff led by John Harbaugh as head coach and Matt Nagy as offensive coordinator.

Mayfield has been a quality starter in Tampa Bay, peaking at fourth among fantasy quarterbacks in 2024 on the back of an unusually high touchdown rate and a jump in rushing. His 2025 slipped as the touchdown rate normalized and his accuracy fell, likely tied to oblique and shoulder injuries, though his rushing stayed strong. A reasonable projection lands between those two seasons: Unlikely to repeat the 2024 touchdown spike, but with a higher rushing floor and a still-strong receiver group even without Mike Evans. New coordinator Zac Robinson brings some uncertainty but has ties to the 2024 scheme, leaving Mayfield outside the top 12 but a strong later-round option who can start in the right matchups.

Mayfield’s 2025 did not go as expected. His touchdown rate returned to his career norm, and his 6.8 yards per attempt was the second-lowest of his career. Further, Mayfield’s accuracy rate fell from 61.3% to 55.9%, while his uncatchable pass rate climbed from 16.0% to 23.1%, and his accuracy on deep and intermediate passes dropped by 12%.

Mayfield dealt with several injuries, including an oblique and a shoulder issue, which likely drove the accuracy dip. He also played through leg injuries but kept running at a strong rate, similar to 2024. That jump came from a higher rushing success rate that lifted his yards per game, along with a big spike in touchdowns.

Mayfield’s career rate of passing attempts becoming touchdowns is 5.0%, but in 2024, it was 7.2%. He also became much more productive as a rusher, averaging 22.2 yards per game after 9.6 the previous year.

That jump came from a higher success rate that lifted his yards per game, along with a large growth in touchdowns. His career rate of passing attempts becoming touchdowns is 5.0%, but in 2024 it was 7.2%. He also became much more productive as a rusher, averaging 22.2 yards per game after 9.6 the previous year.

Expectations for Mayfield should land somewhere between his 2023 and 2024 seasons. His touchdown rate is unlikely to peak like 2024 again, but his rushing floor should stay higher, as it has the past two years. Tampa Bay lost Mike Evans but still has a strong receiver group in Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin and Jalen McMillan. The Buccaneers have a new offensive coordinator in Zac Robinson, though the offense should resemble the strong 2024 version under Liam Coen. Robinson and Coen worked together for several years in Los Angeles, including 2022, when Mayfield was there too.

Mayfield isn't ranked among the top 12 quarterbacks given the uncertainty of a new coordinator, the loss of Evans and how he plays coming back from several injuries. But, he is a strong later-round option who can start when the matchup is right.

His 80.6 receiving grade was eighth-best among running backs with at least 100 routes run, and his 1.86 yards per route run was second-most among backs, just behind Bijan Robinson and just ahead of Christian McCaffrey and Jahmyr Gibbs.

Cleveland completely overhauled its offensive line this offseason, drafting Spencer Fano at left tackle, trading for right tackle Tytus Howard, and signing interior linemen Zion Johnson and Elgton Jenkins. The unit may still project below league average, but it should no longer rank among the NFL's worst.

Sampson should see a substantial increase in playing time and efficiency, which could be enough to make him a flex option against the right opponents.

Love has slipped from seventh to 21st among fantasy quarterbacks in points per game over three seasons, almost entirely because Green Bay's run-heavy approach has cut his passing volume. Love is a safe QB2 with top-10 upside, startable weekly in superflex and matchup-dependent elsewhere. He’s a potential weekly single-quarterback starter if Green Bay’s young pieces develop.

Love has spent the past three seasons as the Packers' starter, ranking seventh (19.4), 16th (16.3) and 21st (16.1) in fantasy points per game. The big reason for the decline has simply been volume. He averaged 34 attempts per game in 2023, and that fell to 28.3 in 2024 and 29.3 in 2025. A small part of that is the games he left with injuries the past two years, but he threw at least 30 times in 13 games in 2023, more than he managed across the two seasons since combined.

Love has been among the highest-graded quarterbacks, his 86.6 passing grade ranking fifth over the past two seasons, but the Packers have had no problem leaning on the run. They rank 31st in dropbacks and fourth in rushing attempts. There is a chance Green Bay throws more this season. Tucker Kraft emerged as one of the league's top receiving tight ends last season before an injury, Christian Watson and Jayden Reed both showed enough promise to earn extensions this offseason, and Matthew Golden is expected to have a larger role in his second year.

The one big concern is the declining offensive line. Green Bay ranked third in pass-block grade in 2024, with Elgton Jenkins, Zach Tom and Rasheed Walker all grading in the 80s, but the team fell to 21st last season. Jenkins and Walker both declined while remaining among its top three linemen in pass protection, and neither is on the roster now. Sean Rhyan and Aaron Banks remain starters despite never posting a PFF pass-blocking grade of 70.0 or better. Jordan Morgan is moving to left tackle full time, which adds uncertainty, and Anthony Belton struggled as a rookie and will need to improve. That uncertainty will make Love's life harder, but it could also mean less effective rushing, which would push the team to throw more.

Love is a top-10 quarterback, and with a different offensive philosophy or better players around him, he would be a top-10 fantasy quarterback. Without that, he is a safe QB2, one who can start weekly in superflex leagues and in the right matchups elsewhere. If some of Green Bay's young skill players improve, Love could become a weekly starter in single-quarterback leagues.

The Packers traded for Willis to serve as a backup, and over two years, he made three starts and saw notable playing time in three other games.

Willis has dropped back to pass just 118 times over the past two years, but his 79.9 PFF passing grade ranks 15th among all quarterbacks. Most important for fantasy, he scrambled on 15.1% of his dropbacks over that span, which leads all quarterbacks. That was notably ahead of Jayden Daniels, Tyrod Taylor, Justin Fields, Drake Maye and Jaxson Dart.

Willis signed with the Miami Dolphins to be their starting quarterback this season. Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley and general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan were both with the Packers before joining Miami. Some passing regression is fair to expect, since Willis won't have the same weapons in Miami that he had in Green Bay. Defenses will also be better prepared for him, since his appearances in Green Bay were often a surprise; because he plays so differently from Jordan Love, defenses weren't ready for him.

Even if Willis’ scrambles per dropback regress somewhat, he should remain among the league leaders in quarterback rushing production, which is a big plus for his fantasy value. Extrapolating his rushing attempts per start and yards per carry in Green Bay, he would have posted 119 rushing attempts and 738 rushing yards over a season, both of which would have led all quarterbacks last year. It's fair not to expect numbers quite that big in Miami, but he could be a fantasy starter if he holds the job and scores enough touchdowns.

Willis is a strong option for anyone willing to wait before adding a second quarterback in redraft leagues.

Every season since has been a strong start followed by injuries, including last year in Washington, where he was WR7 through five weeks before a heel problem and Jayden Daniels‘ absence dropped him to 33rd in points per game. San Francisco brought him back this offseason, and Ricky Pearsall‘s surgery and move to injured reserve clears the way for him to reclaim the Z role. He is worth a mid-to-late-round pick and should start weekly when healthy, which has always been the question.

The 49ers selected Samuel in the second round of the 2019 NFL Draft, and his 2021 campaign was one of the most unique fantasy seasons in NFL history. Through the first nine weeks, he averaged 20.7 PPR points per game. His 882 receiving yards ranked second among wide receivers, and he averaged an absurd 18.0 yards per reception. Beginning in Week 10, San Francisco scaled back his role as a receiver and turned him into one of its primary ball carriers. Samuel averaged 6.2 yards per carry and nearly one rushing touchdown per game the rest of the way, producing 21.7 PPR points per game over that span, the fourth-highest mark among wide receivers.

Samuel's next three seasons followed a familiar pattern: stretches of high-end production interrupted by injuries. In 2022, he was the WR11 through the first seven weeks before a hamstring injury slowed him, and he later suffered MCL and ankle sprains. In 2023, he was the WR18 through five weeks before a shoulder injury sidelined him. He missed two games, eased back into the lineup for one week and then finished as the WR3 from Week 10 through the end of the season. He was the WR11 through two weeks in 2024 before the injuries piled up again. Samuel missed Week 3, and over the first two months of the season he appeared on the injury report with calf, wrist, rib and oblique injuries, as well as an illness. Rib and wrist injuries in January also cost him the final week of the season.

Samuel spent one season with the Washington Commanders after the 49ers were forced to make a difficult financial decision. He was the WR7 through the first five weeks, ranking seventh among wide receivers in receptions and second in rushing attempts. However, a heel injury landed him on the injury report throughout October, and by the time he returned to full health, Jayden Daniels was dealing with injuries of his own and missed much of the remainder of the season. Samuel ultimately finished 33rd among wide receivers in fantasy points per game at 11.8.

He spent most of the offseason as a free agent before returning to San Francisco after Ricky Pearsall's 2025 PCL injury led to lingering knee swelling. Pearsall was soon ruled out for surgery and placed on injured reserve, opening the door for Samuel to reclaim his familiar role at Z receiver. The 49ers had already added Mike Evans at X and Christian Kirk in the slot, leaving Samuel's path to playing time largely unchanged. They also spent a second-round pick on De'Zhaun Stribling, but in the practices between Pearsall's injury and Samuel's signing, veteran Demarcus Robinson filled in at Z. That suggests Stribling is more likely to compete for snaps with Evans or Kirk than with Samuel.

Samuel's level of play has declined over the past two seasons, though injuries have almost certainly contributed. The wear and tear may have caught up to him, and there is a chance he's no longer capable of producing as a consistent fantasy starter. Still, as long as he's healthy, San Francisco's offense gives him a chance to bounce back. The combination of Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy provides one of the league's most favorable environments, and Shanahan has already said he plans to use Samuel as a runner, raising his fantasy floor.

He is worthy of a mid-to-late-round pick. As usual, he should be a weekly fantasy starter if healthy, and health has always been the concern. You can find more statistics and information on his past performance, his competition for touches and how much his teammates and coaches will help or hurt him below.

Addison has been a productive second option opposite Justin Jefferson, but his fantasy value has leaned heavily on touchdowns and on playing with accurate deep-ball quarterbacks, since he is a rare small receiver who wins downfield. Shaky quarterback play tanked him last season, dropping him to 48th in points per game, and this year's likely upgrade under center still isn't a strong deep passer. The bigger blow is the addition of Jauan Jennings, who has graded better than Addison and could take his snaps in two-receiver sets. That extra competition pushes him from a fringe flex to just a late-round option.

Addison has spent the past three seasons as the second option in the Vikings' offense opposite Justin Jefferson. He averaged 53.6 receiving yards per game in his first season and 58.3 in his second. The yardage was modest, but he delivered real fantasy value on the strength of his scoring, with 10 touchdowns as a rookie and nine in 2024. He finished 31st and 24th in fantasy points per game, respectively.

Addison is a rare, small receiver who thrives as a deep threat. Of the 17 wide receivers with at least 60 deep targets over the past three seasons, he is the lightest at 175 pounds and one of only four under 6-foot. Over his first two years, he benefited from Kirk Cousins and then Sam Darnold at quarterback, who rank third and first, respectively, in deep-ball accuracy over that span among the 31 quarterbacks with at least 75 deep attempts.

The Vikings struggled to find consistent quarterback play last season, and that matters more for a deep threat than for an underneath receiver. The instability limited Addison to just two touchdowns, and both of his games over 70 receiving yards came with Carson Wentz at quarterback. He finished 48th in fantasy points per game.

Minnesota's quarterback this season will most likely be Kyler Murray. He should be an upgrade over last year, but his deep-ball accuracy ranks 21st of 31 quarterbacks, and his 7.3-yard average depth of target over the past three years is the fourth-lowest among quarterbacks.

The Vikings also added Jauan Jennings later in free agency. Jennings has graded better than Addison in each of the past three years and could replace him in two-receiver sets, which would further dent Addison's value.

Without Jennings, Addison would still be a clear flex consideration. With him in the mix, he is now just a late-round option.

Pacheco ranked 18th in fantasy points for running backs over the second half of that season. He returned as the starter in 2023, where he averaged 15.3 PPR points per game, ranking 14th-best among backs.

Expectations were high for 2024, but he fractured his fibula, and he hasn't been the same player since. He had PFF grades above 75 in his first two seasons and below 75 in his two most recent seasons. Pacheco signed a one-year, $1.8 million contract with the Detroit Lions this offseason to replace David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs' backup. Montgomery's playing time fell from 47.8% in 2023 to 41.4% in 2024 and 37.1% in 2025.

Expectations were high for 2024, but he fractured his fibula, and he hasn't been the same player since. He had PFF grades above 75 in his first two seasons and below 75 in his two most recent seasons. Pacheco signed a one-year, $1.8 million contract with the Detroit Lions this offseason to replace David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs' backup. Montgomery's playing time fell from 47.8% in 2023 to 41.4% in 2024 and 37.1% in 2025.

In 14-team leagues or leagues with multiple flex spots, Pacheco could keep some flex appeal, given the high-scoring Detroit Lions offense. Pacheco is notably larger than Gibbs, which should lead to at least some goal-line opportunities. His primary value should be as a handcuff, since Pacheco could be the feature back if Gibbs misses time.

Tennessee has a new head coach in Robert Saleh and a new offensive coordinator in Brian Daboll, which could shake up the rotation. Daboll was willing to ride whichever back was more effective at the time during his stint with the New York Giants. Pollard has graded better than Spears as a rusher in both seasons, while Spears has been the better receiver in both.

The most likely outcome is that Spears' role stays similar to his first three seasons, making him a deeper-league flex and a handcuff. The uncertainty around the new staff nudges him ahead of other backs in similar situations, at least until training camp clarifies the usage.

Robinson spent three seasons as the lead rusher for the Washington Commanders, working as an early-down back. At 225 pounds, he is one of the bigger runners in the league, with a high success rate and a 4.1 yards-per-carry average. Backs his size usually aren't much in the receiving game, but he caught 36 passes for 368 yards and four touchdowns in 2023. He finished 21st in fantasy points per game in 2023 and 29th in 2024.

The Commanders traded Robinson to the San Francisco 49ers in the preseason, opting to rely on Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Chris Rodriguez as their early-down backs. Robinson became the primary backup, but Christian McCaffrey didn't miss a game, so Robinson never played more than 30% of snaps in a game. He averaged 5.4 carries per game, with as many as nine some weeks and no touches in others.

He signed with Atlanta this offseason after the departure of Tyler Allgeier, becoming the backup to Bijan Robinson. The Falcons have a new head coach in Kevin Stefanski. His Browns offenses generally leaned on an early-down back as the main runner and a third-down back with less fantasy value. That won't be the setup here, since Bijan Robinson is locked in as the primary passing-down back. It is unclear, though, how the carries will be split between the two, particularly at the goal line.

Brian Robinson is unlikely to carry much standalone value unless Atlanta's offense performs better than expected. He does have notable handcuff value, however. The Falcons' third back is Tyler Goodson, so Brian Robinson would likely get the bulk of the carries if Bijan Robinson were hurt, making him a probable fantasy starter in any matchup from excellent to slightly below average.

Shough flashed as a rookie, averaging 17.6 PPR points per game as a starter with a strong blend of passing and rushing volume, but the production came against a soft schedule and with the Saints leaning heavily on him amid injuries and a thin supporting cast. New Orleans added Travis Etienne and rookie Jordyn Tyson, which should help his efficiency but may also tilt the offense toward more rushing. Shough was drafted 40th overall by the Saints in 2025 and took over as the team's starter partway through Week 8. From Weeks 9 to 18, he averaged 17.6 PPR points per game, 12th among quarterbacks. He had the right combination of volume as both a passer and runner, along with good efficiency for a rookie.

He benefited from an easier-than-average schedule. He faced a top-five defense against fantasy quarterbacks three times and posted two top-10 finishes in those games. In three more against teams in the top half of the league at limiting quarterback fantasy points, he had his other top-10 finish. His remaining three starts came against bottom-half teams, and he failed to crack the top 10 in all three.

The Saints leaned heavily on Shough last season. Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller were both hurt for most of his time as a starter, and the team had traded away Rashid Shaheed and cut Brandin Cooks, leaving it thin at two important positions. New Orleans signed Travis Etienne and drafted Jordyn Tyson, which should help Shough's passing efficiency but could also push the Saints to run more.

Shough's ADP is relatively low because there's usually a reason to prefer other quarterbacks, whether more experience at a high level, a better supporting cast or more rushing upside. The likeliest outcome is he regresses somewhat despite the upgraded weapons, but there's a chance Etienne and Tyson lift the offense to a new level and Shough improves on his 17.6 PPR points per game.

He is a clear example of how deep the quarterback position is this year, and a reason it makes sense to wait at quarterback in single-quarterback leagues. Shough can be drafted in the later rounds and slotted into lineups when the matchup is right.

Dulcich was released shortly before the 2025 season, then claimed by the Dolphins. He made his debut in Week 8 and became a regular part of the Miami offense by Week 9. He never played more than 60% of offensive snaps, but was an effective receiver when given the opportunity. His 2.31 yards per route run ranked third-best among tight ends last season. Dulcich wasn't used much on first down, but his 2.84 yards per route run on second and third downs led the position.

Miami re-signed Dulcich to a $3.25 million deal while moving on from Darren Waller, Julian Hill and Tanner Conner, replacing them with Ben Sims and rookies Will Kacmarek and Seydou Traore. Former head coach Mike McDaniel typically relied on a heavy tight end rotation, while new offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik featured Dalton Schultz in 2023 and 2024.

New general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan pointed to Dulcich as a player poised to make a leap this season. Miami let go of wide receivers Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, filling those spots with third-round rookies and free agents making less than $1.5 million. Dulcich is the favorite to lead Miami in targets.

Johnson finished 12th in fantasy points per game last season at 10.6, but some decline is fair to expect. New Orleans added Noah Fant in free agency and Oscar Delp in the third round, so while Johnson should remain the starter, his snaps might dip slightly. The Saints also drafted Jordyn Tyson in the first round, which pushes Johnson down the target pecking order.

Johnson is a fine, low-upside backup option who can be drafted late.

Jennings spent the first three seasons of his career as the 49ers' slot receiver. That kept Jennings off fantasy radars throughout those three seasons and into the lead-up to 2024.

When Deebo Samuel missed Week 3 of the 2024 season, Jennings stepped in as the Z receiver and caught 11 passes for 175 yards and three touchdowns. He later took over as the 49ers' X receiver with Brandon Aiyuk on injured reserve, averaging a respectable 14.1 PPR points per game over the final nine weeks, 29th among wide receivers.

Aiyuk didn't play in 2025, leaving Jennings as the X receiver, and he posted five receptions for 89 yards and a touchdown in Week 2. At one point early in the season, he said he was playing with high and low ankle sprains, a shoulder at 20% and five broken ribs.

Jennings didn't reach a new deal in San Francisco this offseason, presumably because he couldn't get the terms he wanted, and instead signed a one-year prove-it deal with the Minnesota Vikings. He ran nine times for 104 yards against the New York Giants in Week 8, which eventually helped him take over as the primary backup behind Saquon Barkley. He also received significant time against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 15 and the Washington Commanders in Week 18, reaching 17 and 16 carries in those games, two of his top-five outings.

Bigsby received an 89.1 PFF rushing grade in Philadelphia last season compared to 76.7 by Barkley, while averaging 4.0 yards after contact per attempt compared to 2.7 by Barkley. It would not be surprising if Bigsby's rushing attempts per game see a notable increase this season. However, that will only help fantasy managers in very deep leagues.

It's fair to consider Bigsby the primary handcuff to Barkley, but it's worth noting he has totaled 11 career receptions in 50 games. If Barkley suffers an injury, Will Shipley would also see notable playing time. Bigsby would still be the player to pick up off waivers, but it won't be a one-for-one replacement. His lack of receiving production makes him a worse handcuff option than other backup running backs, despite how good his surrounding cast is.

He tore his ACL and MCL at the end of the 2023 season, and his production hasn't been the same since. He missed the start of 2024, and his receptions dropped to 4.1 per game from 6.3 the year before, with no touchdowns.

Last season was another step in the wrong direction. His receptions per game fell to 3.4, and his 29.2 receiving yards per game was a career low. His PFF receiving grade had held at 77.4 in 2024, in line with past seasons, but it dropped to 62.6 last season.

Part of that could have been the quarterback play. His average depth of target fell to 5.3 after sitting at 7.7 or better every other season, and his targets per route also dropped significantly.

This season, Hockenson will catch passes from Kyler Murray, who leaned on Zach Ertz and Trey McBride in his later years with the Arizona Cardinals. There is a chance that two years removed from the injury, Hockenson is fully recovered and his target rate and average depth return to normal. But there is also a chance he is never the same player, or that he has too much target competition now that Minnesota upgraded its third receiver spot with Jauan Jennings.

Shakir is still worth drafting, since he remains one of the most trusted targets of one of the league's best quarterbacks, but his upside is mostly as a flex option or bye-week fill-in unless his role starts to expand beyond 11 personnel.

A step back on defense would also push the offense to do more, which again means more passing.

Darnold is a fine late-round option with real reason to expect better fantasy production, though the question is how much. He ran for only 95 yards last season, so there is a clear ceiling on his rushing. Even if he doesn't finish among the top 12 fantasy quarterbacks, he can be started in weeks that project as close games rather than clear Seattle wins.

His grades began declining in 2021. His PFF receiving grade has fallen to 66.0 or lower in four of the past five seasons, and his rushing grades have not approached the heights of his rookie or 2020 campaigns. He stayed a top-20 fantasy back from 2022 to 2024 largely on volume, returning to the top 10 in 2024 behind 21.1 touches per game, fifth among running backs.

In 2025, Kamara set career lows in both rushing and receiving grade. The receiving drop is at least partly tied to new head coach Kellen Moore. Moore has coached Ezekiel Elliott, Ekeler and Saquon Barkley in their primes, and all three produced less for fantasy under him than they did before and after. Kamara's receiving yards per game were cut in half, to 16.9. He also began losing snaps to Kendre Miller before Miller suffered a season-ending injury.

The Saints signed Travis Etienne to be their new lead back, which led to several months of speculation around Kamara's future. In mid-July, Kamara renegotiated his contract, assuring him of staying with the Saints. The likely split will be Etienne on early downs and Kamara on passing downs.

Kamara will primarily only have value in deep leagues where there is a chance his receiving production could give him flex value. Outside of that, his value is only as a handcuff.

When kept clean over that span, he averaged 8.1 yards per attempt, tied with Drake Maye and Matthew Stafford for fifth among quarterbacks, but his 5.9 mark under pressure sits right at league average.

The Texans largely reworked the line, signing three free agents and drafting Keylan Rutledge with their first-round pick. Rookie linemen tend to struggle, though, and the two free agents slated to start are on the wrong side of 30 and have already seen their PFF grades slip from their peak. There is a chance the line improves, but perhaps not by much.

Nico Collins has been among the league's best for a few years, Jayden Higgins and Jaylin Noel both flashed as rookies, and Tank Dell should return this season. The other factor, good for the Texans but not for Stroud, is that Houston has one of the league's best defenses, which means it won't allow many points. The addition of David Montgomery should mean more rushing, and the team could lean conservative if that approach is working.

That makes Stroud someone to mostly avoid in single-quarterback redraft leagues, though he remains an intriguing dynasty option. The receivers should stay with him for a few years, the offensive line should trend up rather than down, and the defense is likely to regress at some point. If Stroud improves as a passer on top of that, it is a perfect storm for him to become a much better fantasy option over the next few seasons.

Renfrow left after 2023, Adams was traded in 2024 and Meyers was traded in 2025, which eventually left Tucker atop the Raiders' depth chart. Las Vegas drafted Jack Bech and Dont'e Thornton Jr. in 2025, but neither held a starting job during the season.

Tucker finished last season 38th in fantasy points with 57 receptions for 696 yards and five touchdowns, though he ranked only 49th in points per game. He posted one excellent outing against the Washington Commanders in Week 3, catching eight passes for 145 yards and three touchdowns, but was held under 50 yards in 13 of 17 games.

He faces a bit more competition for targets this season with the free-agent addition of Jalen Nailor. Nailor has graded better than Tucker over their careers, which could push Tucker down the target pecking order, though his playing time is only truly in question if Bech, Thornton or both take a real step forward.

Even with the added competition, Tucker should benefit from an improved offense. The Raiders added Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza at quarterback along with new linemen, led by center Tyler Linderbaum. Tucker is a speedy deep threat who caught 18 passes on deep and intermediate throws last year but also drew 19 uncatchable deep and intermediate targets. Las Vegas quarterbacks posted the second-lowest team accuracy on those throws at 36.8%. Cousins' 47.0% rate over the past two seasons is above league average, and Mendoza ranked third among Power Four quarterbacks last season at 58.7%. Whoever starts, Tucker should see more catchable balls, which should mean more big plays.

Tucker is a fine late-round target, with a chance to be the second-best receiving option behind tight end Brock Bowers on an offense that could be far better than last season. But the offense might not improve, and he could slide down the depth chart if Nailor or one of the second-year receivers earns the quarterback's trust.

Stribling was a surprise early pick at No. 33 and joins a San Francisco receiver room featuring Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel and Christian Kirk. That role is unlikely to produce fantasy value this season, making Stribling only a late-round, deep-league pick. The real angle is 2027, when Stribling projects to take over at X, a spot that has consistently produced with Brock Purdy at quarterback.

Stribling was the 33rd overall pick by the 49ers in the 2026 draft, going much earlier than most draft analysts expected. In college, the 6-foot-2 receiver ran a vertical route tree as a physical player who does not create much separation but wins at the catch point. Our draft guide gave him high marks for his competitive toughness and strength as a blocker.

He joins a receiver room that changed significantly this offseason. Mike Evans was signed in free agency to play X, Deebo Samuel was brought back after a year absense to be their Z receiver, and Christian Kirk was added to work the slot. Stribling's long-term role is likely at X, replacing Evans, who turns 33 before the season starts.

There has been significant speculation about what he does this season. Some beat writers think he will push Kirk for slot work, and those have amplified after Kirk missed time early in training camp. Some speculated he could see time at the Z receiver spot. The most likely outcome is that he rotates with Evans. The 49ers are run-heavy, and Stribling's willingness to block could earn him meaningful early-down snaps. Evans was a fine blocker earlier in his career, but his 38.2 run-block grade over the past four seasons ranks seventh-lowest among receivers with at least 2,000 snaps. It would not be surprising to see Stribling on the field for most 21 personnel snaps and Evans for most out of 11.

That is unlikely to translate to much fantasy value as a rookie. He is still worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues, in case he both handles early downs for Evans and pushes one of the other receivers for playing time. His value should be considerably higher as soon as 2027, as San Francisco's X receiver has consistently produced since Brock Purdy took over at quarterback.

Freiermuth was a reliable, touchdown-scoring tight end who finished 13th at the position as recently as 2024, but his value plummeted in 2025 when Pittsburgh added Jonnu Smith and gave Darnell Washington a bigger role, cutting his snaps to just 50.6%. Both Jonnu Smith and coordinator Arthur Smith are now gone under new head coach Mike McCarthy, which should open up more playing time. The risks are a PFF receiving grade that has slipped over the past three seasons and added target competition from Michael Pittman Jr. and rookie Germie Bernard. He's a fine late-round gamble on your backup, with a chance to return to borderline-starter value.

Freiermuth impressed as a rookie in 2021 with seven touchdowns. He gained 732 receiving yards the following season, ranking ninth among tight ends in fantasy points per game. His 2023 started slowly and was cut into by injuries, but he rebounded in 2024 with another seven-touchdown season, finishing 13th in fantasy points per game.

His fantasy value plummeted in 2025, after offensive coordinator Arthur Smith added Jonnu Smith, a tight end he had worked with on both the Tennessee Titans and Atlanta Falcons. Former third-round pick Darnell Washington also took on a larger role, playing 57.1% of snaps.

That left Freiermuth at just 50.6% of snaps. He had one excellent game against the Cincinnati Bengals, catching five passes for 111 yards and two touchdowns, but he was held to 33 yards or fewer in 14 of 18 games, including the playoffs.

Neither of the Smiths is in Pittsburgh anymore, with Mike McCarthy taking over as head coach. That should mean more playing time for Freiermuth. It sounds like Pittsburgh wants him to be a bigger part of the offense, though his PFF receiving grade has finished below 72.0 in each of the last three seasons after coming in at 74.0 or better in his first two. Pittsburgh also added Michael Pittman Jr. in a trade and Germie Bernard in the second round of the draft, giving him much more target competition from the receiver room.

Freiermuth is a fine late-round tight end if you're looking to gamble on your backup, since there is a chance he returns to borderline fantasy starter status. But there is also a chance he and Washington split the tight end room too evenly, and that Aaron Rodgers focuses on his receivers as he has for most of his career.

Ferguson was the 46th overall pick by the Los Angeles Rams. He joined a crowded tight end room that included Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen. The Rams under Sean McVay have historically been slow to work rookies into their plans. He played only eight offensive snaps over the first five weeks, one of which produced a 21-yard reception.

His role expanded after that single catch, and he played one-third of snaps from Weeks 6-13. That included over half the snaps in 11 personnel on third downs and in 13 personnel, but just under 50% in 12 personnel. He almost never saw the field in 11 personnel on early downs. Higbee missed Weeks 12-17, though it wasn't until Week 14 that Los Angeles trusted Ferguson with a larger role. He played 73.1% of snaps from Weeks 14-17, including 80% of 11 personnel on third downs and every 13 personnel snap.

He caught just 11 passes on the season, but averaged 21.0 yards per reception and scored three touchdowns. The Rams returned all three tight ends and added Max Klare with the 61st overall pick of the 2026 draft. Even so, there is real optimism that Ferguson could break out.

Several people around the team have pointed to the offseason he put together. McVay in particular has spoken glowingly of him, going into detail on how he can be used. The head coach called him a total stud with an incredibly bright future, praising his ability to line up at essentially every skill position on the offense and crediting his maturity, intelligence and instincts. McVay added that the best is yet to come, particularly as a receiver working short, intermediate and downfield.

The deep-threat ability is a plus, but his 18.3 average depth of target was more than six yards higher than any other tight end. If the Rams can mix in easier catches alongside the deep shots, he could be an excellent option. Given the number of weapons in Los Angeles, though, the hesitancy is understandable.

He is a late-round pick in deeper leagues, and it would not be surprising if a big week early in the season turns him into a popular waiver wire target.

Blue was a fifth-round pick by Dallas in 2025. He was a common sleeper target because many thought he had a chance to win the starting job for the Cowboys ahead of veterans Javonte Williams and Miles Sanders. Instead, he was behind both at the start of the year. They had fullback Hunter Luepke, who could also play halfback. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer spoke glowingly of Blue's approach heading into his second season throughout OTAs, saying it's “night and day from where he was last year.” He added that Blue is “going to be a huge part of what we want to do, but he's got to continue to do his part, which he's doing great right now.”

Blue is competing with Davis and Phil Mafah for the backup job, but Dallas seems to want Blue to win it. Williams remains the clear-cut starter, but Blue has handcuff value if he can win the backup role during training camp and the preseason.

Lloyd has been a ghost through two NFL seasons, with hamstring, ankle and appendicitis issues limiting him to a small role in a single regular-season game. Green Bay still appears to view him as the primary backup behind Josh Jacobs, with the depth chart thin enough that no one is clearly ahead of him. The 2024 season was supposed to be a changing of the guard at running back for Green Bay, moving on from Aaron Jones and A.J. Dillon and replacing them with free-agent addition Josh Jacobs and third-round pick Lloyd. Instead, Lloyd suffered a hamstring injury in the preseason that cost him Week 1 of his rookie year. He played in Week 2 but hurt his ankle, landing on injured reserve. He was activated in November, only to develop appendicitis that ended his season.

In 2025, another preseason hamstring injury saw Lloyd miss the entire year. He tried to return but reinjured it and went back on injured reserve. Through two NFL seasons, he has played a small role in one regular-season game.

Despite the string of injuries, the Packers still intend for Lloyd to be their primary backup this season. Chris Brooks and Emanuel Wilson have handled that role recently, but Wilson left for the Seattle Seahawks in free agency. Brooks has been working at fullback in OTAs, suggesting he will be on the field in two-back sets but may not see much single-back work outside of third downs. The only other notable backs on the roster are Pierre Strong Jr., who spent a few years as a Cleveland Browns backup and most of last season on Green Bay's practice squad, and Damien Martinez, a 2025 seventh-round pick by the Seahawks who also landed on the Packers' practice squad late in the year.

There is a path for Lloyd to be a top-10 fantasy running back. Jacobs has typically ranked in that range, and an injury or suspension could hand Lloyd the keys to the backfield, where his production profile is similar. The catch is that Green Bay could just as easily add another back if Jacobs misses time, and Lloyd carries obvious injury risk himself.

That makes Lloyd a deep-league sleeper, though enough training camp and preseason hype could push him into late-round consideration in standard-sized leagues.

The Chargers have not re-signed Allen, opening the door for Harris to play more consistently in three-receiver sets. Given his usage on early downs, there is a chance he ends up with the most playing time of any receiver on the roster.

He posted a 66.6 receiving grade as a rookie, with seven explosive plays and five avoided tackles, and his best statistical game was four catches for 54 yards in Week 16 against the Dallas Cowboys. The Chargers also have a new offensive coordinator in Mike McDaniel, whose Miami Dolphins offense was built on speed. Harris is not slow, but he lacks the speed of the other receivers on the roster.

Harris is a fine speculative late-round pick in deeper leagues, and the first month of the season should tell us whether he is taking to the new role and the new offense.

Jones has been wildly inconsistent for fantasy across his career, and last season's strong 12th-place finish in Indianapolis leaned on five rushing touchdowns and an aggressive, high-aDOT passing profile rather than a real leap in passing quality. His rushing volume has steadily declined, and a ruptured Achilles, even with a Week 1 return expected, makes another five-rushing-touchdown season unlikely. The Colts also lost Michael Pittman Jr. and right tackle Braden Smith without meaningful additions, so the offense could slip. He's a fine second option in superflex but only a deep-bench consideration in single-quarterback redraft leagues.

Jones has spent seven years as an NFL starter, with wildly different fantasy results. He topped out in 2022 with the ninth-most fantasy points per game but has also finished outside the top 30 multiple times. Last season, his first with the Colts, he finished 12th at 18.0 fantasy points per game.

Jones’ 73.2 career PFF passing grade ranks sixth-lowest among the 29 quarterbacks with at least 2,000 dropbacks, and three of the quarterbacks below him are now backups. His single-season grade has hovered between 65.0 and 71.0 most years, so there's little reason to expect a substantial jump in his passing quality.

A big part of Jones’ earlier success was his rushing. In his best season, 2022, he ran 120 times for 708 yards and seven touchdowns. That production has steadily declined since, and last season, he posted career lows of 3.5 attempts and 12.6 yards per game, though he did score five rushing touchdowns.

Those scores helped him to a strong year in Indianapolis, and he also posted a career-high 8.6 average depth of target. That raised Jones’ big-time throw rate but also his turnover-worthy play clip, a combination that generally helps fantasy production.

Jones then suffered a ruptured Achilles that ended his season early. He is expected to be ready for Week 1, but he is unlikely to run for as many touchdowns. The Colts also traded away Michael Pittman Jr. and lost right tackle Braden Smith in free agency without making substantial additions, so the offense could take a small step back.

Jones is a fine second option in superflex leagues but should be drafted in single-quarterback redraft leagues only if the benches are deeper than usual.

Coleman is a unique back at 5-foot-8 and 228 pounds, a slower power runner with excellent tackle-breaking ability and balance. Unlike most backs his build, he has found success as a receiver and has been strong in pass protection, as long as he picks up the right assignment.

The general expectation is that Dobbins, Harvey and Coleman form a three-man committee, though there is a wide range of outcomes for how the snaps get divided. Coleman could see plenty of third-down work given that was Badie's role and he has graded well as a pass protector, and he could take on short-yardage duty as well.

Considering Dobbins' injury history and Harvey's slow start as a rookie, there is a path for Coleman to become the lead option in a one-two punch. But with five backs Denver is comfortable with, even a Dobbins injury could simply produce a different three-back committee. The closest comparison to a back head coach Sean Payton has leaned on is Mark Ingram, who did not post his first 1,000-yard season until his sixth year and his first double-digit touchdown season in his seventh.

Coleman is likely in for a similar slow build, making meaningful fantasy value unlikely this season. Still, given his talent and the unpredictability of Payton's backfield rotations, he is worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues.

The first concern is his lack of receiving production at Indiana. He averaged a solid 1.38 yards per route run in his final season at James Madison before transferring, but he rarely ran routes and was targeted even less often after transferring. His snap rate also never exceeded 45%, as he saw the field primarily on rushing downs.

Our draft guide noted he is better suited to zone-blocking schemes, and the data supports that. He averaged 5.5 yards per attempt on zone runs compared to 4.7 on gap concepts. The guide also noted he has occasionally been a half-step late identifying running lanes in power concepts and that his run game lacks true difference-making creativity.

Black was the only running back selected on Day 2 of the 2026 draft and is a strong fit for Kyle Shanahan's zone-blocking scheme. San Francisco has used a third- through fifth-round pick on a running back in five of the past six drafts, and the first four have not worked out. There is a real chance Black earns the backup job ahead of Jordan James and Isaac Guerendo. Shanahan has said he wants to get Christian McCaffrey help, and Black could fill that role. Given McCaffrey's injury history, which has cost him time in multiple seasons, Black would be a strong fantasy option if he misses time again.

Guerendo tore a pectoral muscle during OTAs and opens training camp on the PUP list, while James fractured his ribs at the start of camp. That could leave Black winning the backup job by default rather than having to earn it in competition. Combined with McCaffrey's injury history and the quality of San Francisco's offensive line, it makes him one of the top handcuff options this season.

Jeudy has spent the past two seasons as the top wide receiver for the Browns after opening his career with four years in Denver. His production in Cleveland has depended almost entirely on who is at quarterback. He posted 1.05 yards per route run, an 18% target rate and three touchdowns on 989 routes without Jameis Winston, compared to 2.50 yards per route run, a 21.8% target rate and three touchdowns on 316 snaps with him. Winston, unfortunately, is now the backup quarterback for the New York Giants.

The two candidates to start for Cleveland this season are Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders. Jeudy has averaged 1.03 yards per route run on a 14.5% target rate with Watson and 1.08 on a 15.6% target rate with Sanders.

To make matters worse, he faces far more competition for targets. Cleveland's top six pass catchers by receptions last season were three running backs, two tight ends and Jeudy. Cedric Tillman was the next receiver on the list at 21 catches. The Browns then spent a first-round pick on K.C. Concepcion and a second-rounder on Denzel Boston, and Isaiah Bond, who joined late last offseason, is expected to have a larger role.

There is some reason to believe those additions could help. Jeudy spent the first five seasons of his career as a Z or slot receiver but primarily played X last season, logging 621 snaps out wide on the line compared to a previous career high of 335. In Cleveland, he has averaged 1.14 yards per route lined up out wide on the line, compared to 1.99 off the line and 1.28 in the slot. On a typical play out of 11 personnel, Boston projects to line up at X, Jeudy at Z and Concepcion in the slot, which puts Jeudy in his best position to succeed. Defenses have also been able to key on him the past two seasons, which becomes harder if the rookies produce.

Jeudy is worth a late-round pick in deep leagues, since he could remain Cleveland's top option despite the additions, and those additions could make him more efficient enough to be a weekly starter. But if one of the rookies takes over or he fails to develop chemistry with his quarterback, he can probably be dropped after a month or two.

Arizona lost each of those nine games, typically by multiple scores, and he had exactly 31 attempts in his other three starts.

The biggest reason to expect a drop in volume is an improved run game. Brissett made his first start last season in Week 6, by which point James Conner and Trey Benson were both out for the year with injuries. Arizona drafted Jeremiah Love, signed Tyler Allgeier, and should have Conner and Benson back, giving it four backs the team values more highly than any Brissett played with last season. So even if Arizona wants to run more, game scripts could still force plenty of late-game passing.
