He isn't worth drafting in most single-quarterback redraft leagues but is a strong waiver target with a good start and a worthwhile upside pick in superflex.

Ward was the first overall pick by the Titans and stepped immediately into the starting lineup. He was expected to have a trio of veteran receivers at his disposal in Calvin Ridley, Tyler Lockett and Van Jefferson, but Ridley played only five full games, catching five passes for 131 yards and two touchdowns in his last healthy one. Head coach Brian Callahan was fired after the sixth game of the season, and Lockett lasted seven games before requesting his release.

That understandably put a damper on Ward's rookie season. The good news is he threw for two touchdowns in each of his final four full games after managing just seven across his first 12. He similarly posted his three best PFF grades near the end of the season.

Ward will have a fresh slate this season, with more options. Tennessee drafted Carnell Tate fourth overall to be its new X receiver and signed Wan'Dale Robinson to play the slot. Ridley is also expected to be healthy, shifting from the clear top option to the third read in the passing game. Brian Daboll is the new offensive coordinator.

In single-quarterback leagues, Ward isn't worth drafting in most redraft formats, but he could easily become a top waiver-wire target with a strong start. In superflex leagues, there are a few veterans he should go ahead of, simply for his upside in a new opportunity.

Otton has played at least 92% of offensive snaps in each of the last three seasons and just signed a three-year, $30 million deal, so the playing time is secure. The production is not, because it has swung almost entirely on health elsewhere: over the last two years he averaged 13.2 PPR points per game in the nine contests Mike Evans and Chris Godwin both missed or barely played, and 7.0 in every other game. New offensive coordinator Zac Robinson is a real point of optimism after what he did with Kyle Pitts, but Evans' departure leaves a deep young receiver group around Godwin rather than a thin one. Leave him on the waiver wire and monitor the receiver injury report.

Otton has been one of the most dependable tight ends in terms of playing time over the last three seasons. He played 96.5% of offensive snaps in 2023, 92.4% in 2024 and 93.2% in 2025. Tampa Bay typically spends a late-round pick on a tight end and did so again this year, so we can expect him to dominate snaps once more. He also signed a three-year, $30 million contract this offseason, which points in the same direction.

His production, however, has largely depended on the health of the wide receivers around him. Over the last two seasons, he averaged 5.9 receptions, 53.3 yards and 0.3 touchdowns in the nine games where Mike Evans and Chris Godwin both missed time or played under 50% of snaps due to injury. He averaged 3.1 receptions, 32.9 yards and 0.1 touchdowns in every other game. That is the difference between 13.2 PPR points per game and 7.0.

The one reason for optimism is new offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, who helped Kyle Pitts reach new heights as a receiver last season. This roster is much deeper at wide receiver than his Atlanta Falcons were, though. Evans is gone, but the Buccaneers have a young core around Godwin that includes Emeka Egbuka, Jalen McMillan, Tez Johnson and Ted Hurst.

He is best left on the waiver wire in most leagues, though he becomes a reasonable add if injuries start piling up in that receiver room.

Gesicki finished 13th among tight ends in 2024 on the strength of five big games, three of which came with Tee Higgins out, but he also had nine games with 2 or fewer yards or three or fewer receptions. The 2025 season was worse, with nothing over 20 yards through five weeks, a pectoral strain costing him the middle stretch, and no real spike even when Higgins missed time again. Cincinnati rotates its tight ends heavily, so he is not guaranteed 12 personnel or third-down work, and Erick All‘s return could cut into the snaps further. He belongs on the waiver wire, though the Joe Burrow connection and the proven ceiling keep him ahead of a few other starting tight ends.

Gesicki ranked 13th among tight ends in fantasy points in 2024, his first season with the Cincinnati Bengals. He had a few spectacular games, highlighted by a 100-yard, two-touchdown performance against the Kansas City Chiefs, and added four more with at least seven receptions and 65 yards. Three of those five big outings came while Tee Higgins was out due to injury. He also had four games with 2 or fewer yards and another five with three or fewer receptions.

He was unable to replicate that success in 2025. He was held to 20 yards or fewer over the first five weeks, then a pectoral strain cost him the middle of the season. He found a little more upon his return, including six catches for 86 yards and a touchdown against the Buffalo Bills. Higgins again missed time late in the year, but Gesicki did not take advantage the way he had in 2024.

Cincinnati rotates its tight ends more than most teams. A receiving tight end usually leads his position group in offensive snaps given how much teams throw, but Gesicki is not always the second tight end in 12 personnel and is not always on the field on third downs, where Drew Sample has at times played for his blocking. If anything, the snaps could thin further with Erick All back.

Gesicki is best left on the waiver wire in most leagues, though he ranks ahead of a few other lead receiving tight ends. He catches passes from Joe Burrow, and he has posted the kind of big games some tight ends never reach.

Tolbert never locked down a consistent role in Dallas, peaking in 2024 before falling behind on the depth chart in 2025, and a move to Miami gives him a genuine opening. The Dolphins gutted their receiver room, moving on from Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle and leaving Malik Washington as the only notable holdover, so Tolbert steps into a wide-open competition among six receivers. Early buzz is encouraging: After OTAs, Tolbert was reportedly separating from the group and working as the X receiver. He projects as Miami's No. 1 target for now, which makes him at least a flex option, though the situation could shift a lot through camp.

Tolbert was a third-round pick by the Cowboys in 2022. He was initially thought to be their potential third receiver, but Noah Brown instead became a top-three receiver for the first time in his career, and Tolbert caught just two passes as a rookie. He eventually worked his way up to third on the depth chart, first behind CeeDee Lamb and Brandin Cooks, then behind Lamb and George Pickens after Pickens replaced Cooks. His best season was 2024, in part because of an injury to Cooks, when he caught 49 passes for 610 yards and seven touchdowns and finished 45th in fantasy points per game.

KaVontae Turpin had always complicated Tolbert's role as the third receiver, and in 2025, Ryan Flournoy overtook him on the depth chart. Tolbert then left for the Miami Dolphins in free agency. Miami moved on from Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, leaving Malik Washington as the only notable holdover from last season and added Tutu Atwell in free agency while drafting Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr.

Training camp and the preseason will go a long way toward determining how much each of those six receivers plays. After OTAs, Omar Kelly noted that Tolbert had put some distance between himself and the rest of the group, and that he was playing the X role, likely also the natural spot for Douglas and Bell. If that holds, Atwell could play the Z and Washington the slot. If Tolbert isn't playing well enough early in the season, Miami could turn to a rookie, though third-round rookie receivers don't often crack the starting lineup.

A lot could change before the season starts, but for now, Tolbert is the top Dolphins receiver to target. Generally, any team's top receiver is worth at least flex consideration.

Perine is Cincinnati's third-down back with little standalone value, but he would likely lead a quality offense's backfield if Chase Brown were to get hurt. That handcuff appeal makes him a late-round option in deeper leagues.

Perine is the third-down back for the Bengals. He spent time with the team from 2020 to 2022, handling third downs behind Joe Mixon, then played a year with the Denver Broncos and another with the Kansas City Chiefs before returning to Cincinnati in 2025.

He has typically been a third-down specialist, but he saw more early-down work as last season progressed, partly because of early struggles from starter Chase Brown. He had two late-season games with 14 carries, both against the Baltimore Ravens, one a blowout win and the other a blowout loss.

Perine is unlikely to hold much standalone value unless Cincinnati is blowing out opponents, but he could carry handcuff appeal. The Bengals' only other notable back is Tahj Brooks, a 2025 sixth-round pick who saw offensive snaps last season only when one of the other two backs was hurt. There is a chance Brooks takes a step forward in year two while Perine slips given his age, though Perine would still likely be the lead back if Brown were to get injured.

That makes him a late-round option in deeper leagues where most backup running backs are rostered, given the quality of the Cincinnati offense and the trust the staff has shown in him.

Gadsden flashed as a rookie, leading all tight ends in fantasy points during a Weeks 6-9 tear before hitting a rookie wall. His 2026 setup is mixed: new coordinator Mike McDaniel runs a faster, more pass-heavy scheme that fits his athletic profile, but the Chargers added Charlie Kolar and David Njoku, crowding the position and threatening his snaps. There's still a breakout path if he settles into the receiving role while the others handle blocking and hybrid duties, though the playing time is a genuine question. He's an intriguing dynasty target for the patient and only a late-round pick in redraft.

Gadsden was a fifth-round pick by the Chargers. He drew more hype from coaches and beat writers than a typical late-round pick throughout training camp, but opened the season as a healthy inactive for the first two weeks. Will Dissly and Tyler Conklin were the top two tight ends on the depth chart, with Tucker Fisk mixed in as a run blocker. An injury to Dissly opened up playing time, and in his first game Gadsden caught five passes for 46 yards on just 22 snaps.

In Week 6, he reached 75% of snaps for the first time and caught seven passes for 68 yards. He followed with seven catches for 164 yards and a touchdown the next week, then two more strong games right after. No tight end scored more fantasy points than Gadsden from Weeks 6 to 9. He then hit a rookie wall, with just one more game over 45 receiving yards and one more touchdown the rest of the way.

The good news is the Chargers have a new offensive coordinator in Mike McDaniel, whose offense is more pass-heavy than predecessor Greg Roman's. His attack with the Miami Dolphins was built on speed, and tracking data shows Gadsden as one of the faster tight ends in the league.

The bad news is that Los Angeles made notable additions at the position. Early in the offseason, the team signed Charlie Kolar to a three-year, $24.3 million contract. He is known for his run blocking, but his 79.3 receiving grade over the past two seasons ranks ninth among tight ends with at least 25 targets. Kolar has exactly 25. Los Angeles also signed David Njoku, who has more than 4,000 career receiving yards with the Cleveland Browns.

That means Gadsden is unlikely to see the playing time fantasy managers would want this year, but it doesn't end his chances of being relevant. Jonnu Smith spent one season in McDaniel's offense, playing just 55% of the snaps yet finishing as the TE4. If Kolar handles the run blocking, Njoku plays a hybrid role and Gadsden takes the receiving work, he could still break out.

He remains an intriguing dynasty option, especially for anyone willing to prioritize the future over this season. In redraft, he is only a late-round target.

The Vikings ranked fifth among fantasy defenses last season, though regression is coming after they led the league with 13 fumble recoveries and added two defensive touchdowns. Minnesota lost four players with more than 500 snaps, including Jonathan Allen, Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Greenard and longtime safety Harrison Smith, while James Pierre was the only notable free-agent addition. The Vikings instead rebuilt through the draft, taking four defenders in the first two days, led by first-rounder Caleb Banks. That should pay off long term, but a slow start is possible while the rookies get up to speed.

The Vikings' defense ranked fifth in fantasy points last season, but is in store for some regression. Minnesota led the league with 13 fumble recoveries and scored two touchdowns, both of which are volatile year to year.

They lost four players who logged more than 500 snaps last season: defensive tackles Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave, edge rusher Jonathan Greenard and longtime safety Harrison Smith, although he hasn't retired yet. Their only notable free-agent addition was James Pierre, who posted a solid 75.1 defensive grade on 643 snaps over the past three seasons.

Minnesota leaned heavily on defense in the draft, taking four defenders across the first two days, led by first-round defensive lineman Caleb Banks. That youth movement should help the Vikings long term, but there could be a slight step back early in the season, depending on how quickly the rookies develop.

The Chiefs allowed the sixth-fewest points in the league last season at 328, yet finished as just the 22nd-ranked fantasy defense because they never made big plays, forcing a league-low six fumbles, scoring no touchdowns or safeties and recording a below-average 35 sacks. Kansas City leaned on the draft to replace them, taking three defenders inside the first 40 picks. More big plays would lift the fantasy outlook, but this is a matchup-based streamer rather than a weekly starter.

The Chiefs were an interesting defense from a fantasy perspective. They allowed the sixth-fewest points last season at 328, but forced a league-low six fumbles, scored no touchdowns or safeties and recorded a below-average 35 sacks. That added up to the 22nd-ranked fantasy defense.

Kansas City suffered significant losses this offseason. Jaylen Watson, Bryan Cook and Trent McDuffie all left after posting PFF defensive grades of at least 74.0 last season. The Chiefs also lost five players in the front seven who each played at least 300 snaps.

Kansas City will turn largely to rookies to fill those gaps, having selected three defenders inside the first 40 picks. If this group can generate more big plays, that would be enough to lift its fantasy value, but this remains a defense to start only in the right matchups.

The Falcons had the 11th-best fantasy defense last season thanks to big plays. They finished second in sacks with 57 and sixth in interceptions with 16. However, they were below average in points allowed.

Atlanta lost two key pieces in the front seven in Kaden Elliss and David Onyemata. Both posted defensive grades above 75.0 over the past three seasons. The Falcons added several players from other teams, but none logged more than 500 snaps last season or graded above 70.0.

There is also concern that James Pearce Jr. will receive a significant suspension following his arrest on domestic violence-related charges. The 2025 first-round pick earned just a 56.1 defensive grade last season. If he is suspended, it mainly means Atlanta's pass rush won't have the same opportunity to improve, though the unit wouldn't necessarily take a step back without him.

Those veteran losses will likely lead to some regression, turning Atlanta from a likely start into a situational one.

Cleveland Browns DST DEF Cleveland Browns

Cleveland finished as the eighth-ranked fantasy defense last season on the strength of 53 sacks — which ranked third — and four defensive touchdowns — tied for the league lead — while grading out as average in most other categories. Jared Verse came back in the Garrett trade, and his 82.2 overall PFF grade makes him the new centerpiece, with Quincy Williams added from the Jets after an injury-shortened 2025. Cleveland had the eighth-ranked fantasy defense last season. Their 53 sacks ranked third, while their four defensive touchdowns tied for the league lead. They were average in points allowed and most other metrics.

The big concern is that they lost their two best players. Myles Garrett, who earned a 93.0 grade last season, was traded to the Los Angeles Rams. Linebacker Devin Bush, who posted an 87.6 grade, signed with the Chicago Bears. No one else on the defense graded above 80.0.

Cleveland received Jared Verse in the Garrett trade, and his very respectable 82.2 grade makes him the Browns' new top defender. They also added Quincy Williams from the New York Jets, who has graded well in the past but is coming off a down 2025 season.

Those losses will likely leave Cleveland as a below-average defense, one worth starting only in the right matchup.

Mendoza was the No. 1 overall pick and the best pure passer in his class, but several factors keep him below the typical top selection in fantasy. He landed with a Raiders team that graded near the bottom of the league on offense, offers little of the rushing upside that fuels most recent first-round quarterbacks and ranks in the back third of recent first-rounders in PFF passing grade. Typically, quarterbacks taken first overall land higher in redraft and dynasty rookie rankings, but a few factors push Mendoza below the usual No. 1 pick.

Mendoza joins the Raiders, who posted the third-lowest team offensive grade last season. Ideally, they will have left tackle Kolton Miller back at full strength and will add reinforcements to the receiver room and offensive line this offseason. The better the Raiders look, the more he could climb these rankings.

He also lacks the rushing upside of most recent first-round quarterbacks. Based on PFF tracking data, he ranks among the bottom three in athleticism and top speed among first-round quarterbacks over the past three seasons, alongside Bryce Young and Cam Ward. Stroud, Michael Penix Jr. and Kenny Pickett, so all three of these low-athleticism passers grade poorly as runners.

Mendoza joins the Raiders, who posted the third-lowest team offensive grade last season. Claiborne is an undersized, change-of-direction rookie who profiles as a pass-catching specialist in the mold of Justice Hill, a role that has produced fantasy value for players like Kenneth Gainwell. He landed in Minnesota behind Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason, with Jones as his more direct competition for receiving work. However, Jones' age, recent injury history and declining efficiency open a path for Claiborne to take over that role at some point this season. Even then, Claiborne would likely only absorb part of Jones' workload rather than inherit it outright, capping his redraft value. A strong rookie season could set him up for a bigger role in 2027, when neither Jones nor Mason is under contract. He's a fine dynasty stash, best drafted only in deep redraft leagues.

Claiborne is a small, speedy running back with great change-of-direction ability. Our draft guide compared him to Justice Hill and mentioned his upside as a receiving running back. He is not expected to become a three-down back, but there are plenty of receiving specialists at the position who have found fantasy value. For example, Kenneth Gainwell finished last season as RB16 while ranking fourth in receptions (73) and 47th in rushing attempts (114).

Claiborne landed with the Vikings in the sixth round, where he will likely start his career behind Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason on the depth chart. Mason has served more of an early-down role throughout his career, while Jones has played on third downs, and significantly on early downs as well, making Jones his primary competition.

The 31-year-old running back accepted a pay cut to remain with the Vikings, and he has missed significant time in two of the last three seasons. His rushing efficiency and receiving production have both declined in recent years. There is a reasonable chance Claiborne will be the Vikings' lead receiving back at some point this season.

In that scenario, chances are Claiborne would only take part of Jones' playing time, with Mason also taking a larger role. This makes it unlikely Claiborne will be fantasy viable, even in the scenario of a Jones injury. However, neither Jones nor Mason is under contract in 2027. The better Claiborne plays this season, the larger his role can be in 2027. He is a fine dynasty stash, but should only be drafted in deep redraft leagues.

Young has spent the past three seasons as the Panthers' starting quarterback after being the first overall pick of the 2023 draft. He had a rookie year to forget and was briefly benched in 2024 before returning and ending the season with a 75.9 PFF offensive grade. He regressed slightly in 2025 to a 71.0 grade, but better weapons around him led to better fantasy production.

The Panthers drafted Tetairoa McMillan eighth overall, and he matched Adam Thielen's production from Young's rookie season. Jalen Coker emerged as the best second option Young has had in his young career, and Rico Dowdle put up the most receiving yards by a Panthers running back in three seasons.

All of that added up to the 28th-most fantasy points per game among quarterbacks last season. The starters below him either lost their jobs, are competing for jobs, changed teams or were Cam Ward as a rookie.

Carolina made minimal changes to the offense this offseason. Jonathan Brooks replaces Dowdle in the backfield, first-round pick Monroe Freeling may not contribute much as a rookie, and the team added a little competition for Xavier Legette at the third receiver spot.

Rodgers is well past his MVP peak, averaging fewer than 16 fantasy points per game in each of his past two seasons while posting the lowest full-season passing grade of his career in 2025. A reunion with longtime head coach Mike McCarthy, along with the additions of Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard, should keep him from the bottom tier of fantasy quarterbacks, but at 42 years old, a meaningful rebound is unlikely. Rodgers is strictly a superflex option, with the potential to provide steady QB2 production. The concern is that his continued decline could leave him unstartable even in that format.

Rodgers was once a top NFL quarterback, with four MVPs and several excellent fantasy seasons. Those days are behind him, though. He averaged 14.8 points per game in his final season in Green Bay, missed nearly all of 2023, averaged 15.7 in his one full season with the New York Jets, and 14.6 in his first season with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Nearly every starting quarterback he beat in fantasy production last season has either changed teams, is fighting for a starting job, or is significantly younger with room to improve.

The good news is Rodgers has reunited with Mike McCarthy, his longtime coach in Green Bay during his peak. Pittsburgh also invested in the receiver room, adding Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard.

Bernard is a versatile, well-rounded receiver with no glaring weaknesses but no elite trait either, and he landed in Pittsburgh behind D.K. Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. He will battle Roman Wilson for the third receiver job, and recent history suggests Day 2 rookies do not always seize those roles immediately. Even if Bernard wins it, the volume likely will not be there for fantasy without an injury ahead of him. He is a speculative late-round pick in deep leagues with more appeal in dynasty, given the uncertainty around both veterans' futures in Pittsburgh.

Bernard is a well-rounded receiver. There is no area of his game where he would be considered the best in the 2026 draft class, but there are also no obvious weaknesses. He is capable of playing all three receiver spots, making him a versatile chess piece for an offense.

He was the 47th overall pick by the Steelers, a team that desperately needed receiver help last season. D.K. Metcalf remains atop the depth chart, but Pittsburgh did not retain Calvin Austin III, Adam Thielen, Marquez Valdes-Scantling or Scotty Miller. The Steelers then traded for Michael Pittman Jr. to serve as their second option.

Bernard will compete with Roman Wilson for the third receiver spot. Wilson missed nearly all of his rookie season in 2024 with an injury and managed only 12 receptions last year. Fantasy managers tend to expect Day 2 rookies to immediately leapfrog veterans, but that is not always how it goes. It took Luther Burden III half of last season to pass Olamide Zaccheaus, Jayden Higgins never fully surpassed Xavier Hutchinson, and both Tre Harris and Jack Bech spent most of last season fourth on their depth charts.

Bernard is a speculative late-round pick in deeper leagues until he shows he has locked down the third receiver job. Even then, he is unlikely to see enough volume to matter for fantasy barring an injury to Metcalf or Pittman. His long-term value is stronger, since it is unclear whether either veteran is part of Pittsburgh's future.

Smith returns to where his career began, taking over as the Jets‘ starting quarterback after three productive seasons in Seattle and a disappointing year in Las Vegas. His peak came in 2022, when he finished fifth among fantasy quarterbacks, though his fantasy points per game declined in each of the following seasons. Last year was another step back, as his passing yards per game dropped by 40 from his 2023 mark following the midseason trade of Jakobi Meyers, a knee injury to Brock Bowers and the firing of offensive coordinator Chip Kelly. New York's supporting cast, led by Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell and rookies Omar Cooper Jr. and Kenyon Sadiq, is stronger than what he had in Las Vegas but falls short of the prime D.K. Metcalf-Tyler Lockett pairing, and at 36 years old, Smith no longer offers much rushing upside. He is best avoided in single-quarterback redraft leagues and profiles as a safe, low-end QB2 in superflex formats.

Smith spent two years as a starter for the New York Jets, followed by seven seasons as a backup. In 2022, he took over as the Seattle Seahawks' starter and held the job for three years. He followed that with one season in Las Vegas, and now he is back with the Jets as their starter.

Smith played well during his three seasons in Seattle, posting an 88.8 offensive grade. He ranked fifth in fantasy points in 2022, although his 18.5 points per game ranked only eighth. He fell to 24th in points per game in 2023 and 15th in 2024. The 2023 dropoff was simply fewer yards per game, along with a slight decline in passing efficiency and fewer rushing attempts.

Smith played well during his three seasons in Seattle, posting an 88.8 offensive grade. He ranked fifth in fantasy points in 2022, although his 18.5 points per game ranked only eighth. In New York, his passing weapons will be Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell and rookies Omar Cooper Jr. and Kenyon Sadiq. That is better than what he had in Las Vegas, but a step down from D.K. Metcalf and Tyler Lockett at their best, unless the rookies contribute immediately.

Smith will be 36 before the end of the season. It's unlikely his rushing will match the peak of his career, and unless the offense plays much better than expected, his passing volume will be hard-pressed to reach his Seattle levels. He is a quarterback to avoid in redraft leagues and a safe, low-end QB2 in superflex.

Now in Atlanta, he is competing with Michael Penix Jr., who is recovering from a partially torn ACL, though Tagovailoa appears to be the favorite to open the season as the starter even if the Falcons still view Penix as their long-term answer. Tagovailoa spent the first six seasons of his career as the lead quarterback of the Miami Dolphins. He earned an 81.6 passing grade over that span, which ranked 20th among quarterbacks. Miami decided to move on, leaving Tagovailoa with the Atlanta Falcons. Atlanta drafted Michael Penix Jr. with the eighth overall pick in 2024, and he is recovering from a partially torn ACL. Tagovailoa has strong weapons in Atlanta with Drake London and Kyle Pitts. However, Kirk Cousins had those same weapons over the final seven weeks last season and averaged just 14.0 fantasy points per game.

Tagovailoa is a QB2 option in superflex leagues, but only for as long as he holds the starting job.

Williams is a polished slot receiver out of Clemson whose profile, smaller size and effective 11-personnel-only usage among comparable players typically caps fantasy ceiling, though Zay Flowers and Jaylen Waddle show that outcome isn't universal. He appears to have won the slot job over Jaylin Lane and Luke McCaffrey in a Washington receiver room behind Terry McLaurin, but Washington has kept him mostly in the slot through the start of OTAs despite his outside experience. Williams is the only Commanders receiver besides McLaurin worth fantasy consideration this season, and his outlook hinges entirely on whether he earns outside-receiver snaps by Week 1. If he does, he becomes a popular sleeper before his ADP catches up, and if he doesn't, an expanded role likely isn't coming during the season.

Williams was a third-round pick by the Washington Commanders. Our draft guide called him "a quick, precise slot-only receiver with strong separation metrics but a low average depth of target." His PFF receiving grade improved each season and reached a solid 80.3 in his final year at Clemson.

Typically, a player of his profile doesn't lead to a lot of fantasy success. He measures at 5'11", 190 pounds. Zay Flowers and Jaylen Waddle have been consistent fantasy starters at smaller sizes, but most other wide receivers of a similar size, like Josh Downs, Wan'Dale Robinson and Jayden Reed, have typically been stuck in 11 personnel only. Washington was right around league average in how often they used 11 personnel last season. They have a new offensive coordinator in David Blough, but he was on the coaching staff each of the last two seasons.

Williams joins a particularly crowded wide receiver room, where the only sure thing is that Terry McLaurin is one of the starting wide receivers. Washington has spent a middle-round draft pick on a slot receiver in each of the last three seasons. Williams appears to be the favorite over Jaylin Lane and Luke McCaffrey. Washington kept Treylon Burks from last season while adding Dyami Brown and Van Jefferson. Washington is also expected to add Brandon Aiyuk when he becomes available.

The big question is when and if Williams will receive opportunities as an outside receiver, or if he will be stuck in the slot. When he was first drafted, head coach Dan Quinn brought up his experience and ability to play both outside and in the slot. During the start of OTAs, Washington kept him mostly in the slot.

Williams is the only other wide receiver outside of McLaurin that fantasy managers should consider this season because of his upside. Ideally, he will be given opportunities outside of the slot in training camp and the preseason. If that happens, he will become everyone's favorite sleeper wide receiver until his ADP rises. If he doesn't get these opportunities by Week 1, it's unlikely his role will grow to include those snaps during the season.

Sanders went from a projected top pick to a fifth-round selection in the 2025 NFL Draft and averaged 13.2 fantasy points per game over his final seven starts, hampered by both low passing volume and a league-worst 45.5 offensive grade among quarterbacks with at least 300 snaps. Cleveland has since invested heavily in the offense, drafting wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston in the first two rounds while rebuilding the offensive line, and the trade of Myles Garrett could force the Browns into more pass-heavy game scripts. If Sanders wins the starting job, there is a path to QB2 value in superflex leagues. The challenge is that he is competing with Deshaun Watson, and with two first-round picks in next year's draft, Cleveland remains well positioned to select another quarterback, leaving no one's hold on the job particularly secure.

Sanders was a fifth-round pick by the Browns in 2025, after significant speculation he could go among the top few picks of the draft. Cleveland gave him a chance to start over the final seven weeks of the season.

He averaged 13.2 fantasy points per game over that stretch. Part of the problem was volume, as he threw 25 times or fewer in four games, including three victories. Efficiency was an issue too. His 45.5 offensive grade was the lowest among all quarterbacks with at least 300 snaps last season.

The good news is that Cleveland has invested heavily in the offense. The Browns used one first-round pick on wide receiver KC Concepcion and a second-rounder on Denzel Boston, and they completely reworked the offensive line. If Sanders is the starter, we can expect improved production. With Myles Garrett gone, Cleveland may also need to throw more often. All of that points to more fantasy value, potentially pushing Sanders into QB2 territory in superflex leagues.

The problem is that the starting job isn't assured. He is currently competing with Deshaun Watson, who missed all of last season recovering from two Achilles surgeries. The Browns also have two first-round picks next year and will likely draft a quarterback unless Sanders or Watson works out in a big way. Whoever wins the job in Week 1 might not hold it into the second half if the team isn't winning. That makes Sanders harder to draft than the 30 or so quarterbacks with clearer paths to starting.

Indianapolis added eight defenders from other teams who played at least 250 snaps last season, and none of them graded above 64.0. The Colts also drafted linebacker CJ Allen in the second round and safety AJ Haulcy in the third, and both are contenders to start.

The biggest reason for optimism is a full season of Sauce Gardner. Indianapolis traded for him midseason but got only two full games out of him before an injury in his third, followed by a limited role in his Week 17 return. Even so, the Colts should be an average defense again this year.

Fields is a 6'4", 222-pound X receiver taken 74th overall, with excellent hands, blocking and toughness that fit a John Harbaugh offense, though his college receiving grades were good rather than great and he profiled better against zone than man. He lands in a crowded New York room behind Malik Nabers, Darius Slayton and a wave of free agent additions, with Slayton his most direct competition and a potential Beckham roster spot further squeezing his rookie snaps. His best path to value is a breakout if one of the non-Nabers receivers emerges, but with Mooney or Austin the likelier beneficiaries of any Nabers absence, Fields is best viewed as a deeper-league dynasty stash than a redraft contributor.

Fields is a 6'4", 222-pound X receiver who was drafted with the 74th overall pick by the Giants. Per our draft guide, he has excellent hands, with great blocking and toughness, which fit a John Harbaugh offense. His grades were consistently decent throughout college, going from a 72.7 receiving grade in 2023 to 75.8 in 2025. While most X receivers excel against man, Fields performed better against zone defenses.

Fields joins a crowded wide receiver room in New York. Malik Nabers and Darius Slayton return to the team, while New York added Darnell Mooney, Calvin Austin III, JuJu Smith-Schuster and Odell Beckham Jr. in free agency. Three of the four free agent additions had worked with either new head coach John Harbaugh or new offensive coordinator Matt Nagy in a previous season.

His primary competition for playing time will likely come from Slayton, who has been the Giants' X receiver in recent seasons. If Beckham makes the roster, that also would not be a good sign for Fields' playing time as a rookie.

If Nabers is able to play early in the season, it will be difficult to trust any of the other Giants receivers, but if any one of them were to break out, Fields would have the most upside. If Nabers misses time, then Mooney or Austin would likely benefit the most, and the impact on Fields would be minimal. The most likely scenario is that Fields spends his rookie season as a rotational backup.

New Orleans Saints DST DEF New Orleans Saints

The Saints ranked 12th in fantasy points last season, helped by three defensive touchdowns and 10 fumble recoveries, which tied for fourth-most, though they were only average in points allowed against one of the league's easiest schedules. New Orleans then lost linebacker Demario Davis and his 89.2 grade over the past three seasons, along with starting cornerback Alontae Taylor to Tennessee. Kaden Elliss returns from Atlanta to take over for Davis, and his 75.4 three-year grade is solid without matching what Davis provided, while the 2025 mid-round picks will be counted on at cornerback. Some regression is coming regardless of the roster, and these changes tilt New Orleans toward a step back.

The Saints defense ranked 12th in fantasy points last season. They were one of five teams with at least three defensive touchdowns, and their 10 fumble recoveries tied for the fourth-most. However, they were only average in points allowed against one of the most favorable schedules in the league.

New Orleans lost longtime linebacker Demario Davis, who posted an 89.2 defensive grade over the past three seasons. They also lost starting cornerback Alontae Taylor to the Tennessee Titans.

The Saints replaced Davis with Kaden Elliss from division rival Atlanta. His 75.4 grade over the past three seasons is respectable for a starter but not at Davis' level. New Orleans will largely rely on its 2025 mid-round picks to replace Taylor.

Even if this defense were unchanged, some regression would be expected given how it generated its fantasy points. The offseason changes make a step back more likely than a step forward.

Cincinnati Bengals DST DEF Cincinnati Bengals

The Bengals yielded the third-most points and second-most yards in the league last season, though 13 interceptions kept them respectable in fantasy. Trey Hendrickson‘s departure is the biggest loss, but he missed most of last season anyway, and the three other players gone with at least 300 snaps all graded at 64.0 or worse. Cincinnati then went shopping, adding Dexter Lawrence II, Boye Mafe and Bryan Cook, who may now be the three best players on the defense. With a young roster around them, the Bengals should improve, and there's a path to an above-average unit if the younger players develop.

The Bengals allowed the third-most points (492) and second-most yards (6,475) last season. They outperformed that from a fantasy perspective thanks to an above-average 13 interceptions.

Cincinnati's biggest loss was pass rusher Trey Hendrickson, who missed most of last season with an injury. They lost three other players with at least 300 snaps, but all of them graded at 64.0 or worse. There is little reason to expect this defense to be worse in 2026.

The Bengals made three notable additions, headlined by Dexter Lawrence II and his 91.9 defensive grade over the past three seasons. Edge rusher Boye Mafe and safety Bryan Cook both posted PFF grades above 70.0 last season and over the past three seasons. An argument could be made that these are the three best players on Cincinnati's defense.

The Bengals are relatively young outside of those additions and defensive tackle B.J. Hill, so the rest of the unit could also improve with experience. Expect some improvement from the free-agent additions, and this could be an above-average unit if some of the younger players work out.

Simpson was a genuine stunner at 13th overall, going roughly a round earlier than expected after just 15 college starts. Our draft breakdown pegged him as a solid starter who could use another year to refine his decision-making and pocket feel, and he'll get exactly that behind reigning MVP Matthew Stafford. The situation he eventually inherits is about as good as it gets, with Sean McVay running an offense that graded a league-best 92.0 last season even excluding quarterback play. That makes Simpson a borderline single-quarterback league starter and a clear superflex one whenever he takes over, but with Stafford entrenched and Stetson Bennett IV possibly holding the backup job, he has almost no redraft value. In dynasty superflex, he's worth a first-round rookie pick.

Simpson was a surprise selection for Los Angeles at 13th overall, as many expected him to go late in the first round or early in the second. He started only 15 games in college, beginning that lone season strongly before struggling as it progressed. Our draft breakdown called him a solid starter who ideally would have had another year to improve his decision-making and develop a better feel in the pocket.

He will get that year, though he'll have to make those gains in practice rather than in games. Matthew Stafford was the NFL's MVP last season and will be the Rams' starter for as long as he is healthy, so Simpson will sit for at least one year. Stafford is 38 and may not be in Los Angeles much beyond 2026, especially if Simpson develops.

Whenever he does take over, Simpson will be in an excellent situation. Sean McVay is arguably the best coach in the NFL, and the Rams posted by far the highest offensive grade in the league last season at 92.0, even with quarterback play excluded. Simpson would be a borderline fantasy starter in single-quarterback leagues once he wins the job, and a clear one in superflex.

Simpson has almost no redraft value, as there's a chance Stetson Bennett IV holds the backup job and Simpson focuses entirely on 2027 and beyond. In dynasty superflex leagues, he is worthy of a first-round rookie pick given his upside in the Rams' offense.

Stowers brings rare athleticism and production for a tight end, posting a 91.4 career receiving grade at Vanderbilt that tops recent first-round tight ends and testing in the 95th percentile across several combine drills, though his sub-240-pound frame is the swing concern, even as recent undersized tight ends like Harold Fannin Jr. have thrived. He lands behind Dallas Goedert in Philadelphia for a season, but with Goedert turning 32 and on a reduced deal, Stowers looks like the heir apparent for 2027 and beyond in an offense that has produced a top-12 fantasy tight end for seven straight years. This season is the wait, though, since he could easily rank third in snaps at the position behind blocking-oriented options, making him a real impact player only on a Goedert injury or a standout camp, and a top tight end handcuff in deep enough leagues.

Stowers is an athletic former quarterback who transitioned to tight end and produced at a high level over his final two seasons at Vanderbilt. That included 100-yard games against Texas, Auburn and Alabama, along with two nonconference opponents. His 91.4 career PFF receiving grade is higher than that of recent first-round picks such as Tyler Warren and Colston Loveland, and notably higher than fellow rookie Kenyon Sadiq's. From a testing standpoint, he ranked in the 95th percentile or better in the 40-yard dash, 20-yard shuttle, vertical jump and broad jump.

The primary concern with Stowers is his size. He was listed at 235 pounds in college and measured 239 pounds at the combine. Historically, tight ends under 240 pounds have rarely made a significant fantasy impact. However, Juwan Johnson, Harold Fannin Jr. and Oronde Gadsden II are all under that threshold and just delivered three of the most productive seasons by players of that size in the past 20 years in terms of receiving yards.

Stowers joins the Philadelphia Eagles, where he will be Dallas Goedert's backup for one season, although he will have a shot to cut into Goedert's playing time. Goedert took a pay cut to stay with Philadelphia, and he will be 32 by the end of the season. This makes Stowers the likely starter in 2027. Goedert has ranked among the top 12 tight ends in fantasy points per game in each of the last seven seasons, and Stowers could follow in those footsteps and be a fantasy starting tight end for several seasons.

Expectations should be much lower for Stowers this season. While he should receive some playing time, it wouldn't be surprising if he sees the third-most offensive snaps at the position, with either Grant Calcaterra or Johnny Mundt used for their run blocking. It will either take an injury to Goedert or an amazing camp by Stowers for him to make an impact in fantasy leagues this year. However, if you're in a deep enough league where some backup tight ends are rostered, he should be considered one of the top tight end handcuffs.

New York Giants DST DEF New York Giants

The Giants were the fifth-worst fantasy defense last season and reshaped the roster accordingly, trading Dexter Lawrence II for a first-round pick while losing Bobby Okereke, Cor'Dale Flott and Dane Belton, all of whom played more than 700 snaps. New York brought in 16 players who took a snap elsewhere last season, though only a handful matter. That group is led by defensive tackle DJ Reader, plus fifth overall pick Arvell Reese. Reese is slated to start immediately, but rookie linebackers rarely transform a defense, and replacing Lawrence with Reader looks more like a downgrade than an upgrade. There isn't much reason to expect a significantly better unit this season.

The Giants had the fifth-worst defense by fantasy points last season. Like most units that ranked near the bottom, New York made several changes this offseason.

Their biggest loss was Dexter Lawrence II, whom they traded for a first-round pick. Linebacker Bobby Okereke, cornerback Cor'Dale Flott and safety Dane Belton all played more than 700 snaps and are no longer on the roster.

New York added 16 players who took at least one snap for another team last season, though only five are notable. The most significant is defensive tackle DJ Reader, who posted a 76.5 defensive grade over the last three seasons. The Giants also used their fifth overall pick on linebacker Arvell Reese.

Unless Reese makes an immediate impact, there isn't much reason to expect a significantly better season from this defense. If anything, he could struggle the way most rookies do, and the swap from Lawrence to Reader may prove to be a downgrade.

Miami ranked below-average in every major defensive metric last season without ever bottoming out. The roster has since been gutted, particularly in the secondary, where all five of the Dolphins’ top defensive backs by snap count are gone. The replacements are thin, with former Titans cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. the only free-agent addition who started last season and everyone else compiling 350 snaps or fewer, though first-round cornerback Chris Johnson should start right away. Miami ranked below average in every major defensive metric last season but was rarely among the bottom five.

The Dolphins have made several changes, particularly in the secondary. Jack Jones, Rasul Douglas, Minkah Fitzpatrick, Ashtyn Davis and Ifeatu Melifonwu were their top five defensive backs in snaps, and none of them remain on the roster.

Miami added just one player in free agency who started last season, former Tennessee Titans cornerback Darrell Baker Jr., while the rest of their free-agent additions played 350 snaps or fewer. The Dolphins also drafted cornerback Chris Johnson with the 27th pick.

The primary reason for optimism is new head coach Jeff Hafley, but it might take time to see notable improvement. This is a defense to avoid at the start of the season.

Washington Commanders DST DEF Washington Commanders

No defense allowed more yards than the Commanders last season at 6,533, and they ranked among the bottom six in points allowed and fantasy points. Six players with at least 200 snaps are now free agents, all of them 30 or older, including future Hall of Famers Bobby Wagner and Von Miller. The headline addition is seventh overall pick Sonny Styles, with free agency bringing high-snap but low-graded players in Nick Cross, Amik Robertson and K'Lavon Chaisson, plus better-graded part-timers in Leo Chenal and Tim Settle. The youth movement should pay off eventually, but it isn't likely to show up in the standings this season, so avoid Washington unless it outperforms expectations.

No defense allowed more yards than the Commanders last season at 6,533. They also ranked among the bottom six teams in points allowed and fantasy points.

They had six players with at least 200 snaps last season who are all free agents, and all six are at least 30 years old. That list includes two future Hall of Famers in Bobby Wagner and Von Miller.

Their biggest addition is rookie linebacker Sonny Styles, taken with the seventh overall pick. Washington also made several free-agent additions. Safety Nick Cross, cornerback Amik Robertson and defensive end K'Lavon Chaisson all played more than 800 snaps last season but graded below 60.0. Linebacker Leo Chenal and defensive tackle Tim Settle both graded in the 70s, though with fewer than 500 snaps each.

Washington's youth movement on defense should help in the long run, but it might not translate to a better finish in the short term. They are a defense to avoid unless they play better than expected.

Las Vegas Raiders DST DEF Las Vegas Raiders

The Raiders allowed the eighth-most points last season but ranked third-worst in fantasy because they generated so few big plays. Las Vegas lost linebackers Devin White, Elandon Roberts and Jamal Adams to free agency along with Kyu Blu Kelly and Tyree Wilson, then spent heavily to rebuild the front seven with Nakobe Dean, Quay Walker, Kwity Paye and Taron Johnson before adding five more defenders in the first five rounds of the draft. The money was real, but the grades are not: Dean leads the group at 72.9 over the past three seasons, and none of the additions profile as difference-makers. The unit should be modestly better, without the kind of immediate leap other bottom-tier defenses might make.

The Raiders allowed the eighth-most points last season, but a lack of big plays dropped them to third-worst from a fantasy perspective.

Most teams near the bottom completely overhauled their starting lineups, and Las Vegas spent heavily to do the same, though the additions don't look like difference-makers by PFF grade. Linebackers Devin White, Elandon Roberts and Jamal Adams each played more than 400 snaps last season and are now free agents. Cornerback Kyu Blu Kelly and defensive end Tyree Wilson are also gone.

Las Vegas added four free agents with at least 300 snaps last season. The most notable is linebacker Nakobe Dean, who posted a 62.2 grade last season and a 72.9 mark over the past three. Quay Walker, Kwity Paye and Taron Johnson were also brought in to start. The Raiders then added five defenders in the first five rounds of the draft, though it's unclear whether any will start.

Las Vegas should be slightly better with those additions, and one or two rookies could pay off immediately. Still, unlike other defenses that finished near the bottom last season, there isn't much reason to expect significant improvement right away.

New York Jets DST DEF New York Jets

The Jets scored the fewest fantasy points of any defense last season at 47.0, a full 12 behind the second-worst, and they traded away their two best players in Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner at midseason. New York then overhauled the roster, letting eight veterans who all graded below 64.0 walk while adding eight players with at least 380 snaps last season, headlined by T'Vondre Sweat, David Onyemata, Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick, who each graded at 79.0 or better. The draft brought more help, with edge rusher David Bailey going second overall and cornerback D'Angelo Ponds in the second round. Last season's numbers mean almost nothing here, and while a below-average unit is the reasonable expectation, the range of outcomes is unusually wide.

The Jets defense scored the fewest fantasy points last season at 47.0, notably 12 fewer than the second-worst and 28 fewer than the third-worst. They also traded their two best players, defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and cornerback Sauce Gardner, at midseason.

New York let another eight veterans leave this offseason who played at least 100 snaps last year, though all eight graded below 64.0.

The Jets made several additions on defense, bringing in eight players with 380 or more snaps last season. Defensive tackles T'Vondre Sweat and David Onyemata, linebacker Demario Davis and safety Minkah Fitzpatrick all posted grades of 79.0 or better. New York also used high draft picks on that side of the ball, including second overall pick David Bailey and second-round cornerback D'Angelo Ponds.

This defense will be almost entirely new, so last season's numbers have little bearing on how 2026 plays out. With so many moving parts, a below-average unit is the reasonable expectation, though there is a chance it plays well if everything comes together.
